Out of Bounds: sexual exploitation in counselling and therapy by Janice Russell. Published by Sage, London, 1993; 159 pages; £10.95.

Francesca Raphael

Francesca Raphael

London

Francesca Raphael  

The author is to be applauded for venturing into the difficult and murky territory of sexual exploitation of clients by therapists and counsellors. Her two main objectives were firstly ‘… to inform the practitioner about what sexual exploitation within this context is and how it might occur… ‘and secondly’… to look at how the professions involved might begin to consider the subject and to introduce strategies to deal with and prevent such exploitation as far as possible.’ It seemed to me that she was more successful in the former than the latter for a variety of reasons.

Early on, the author quotes from clients' verbal accounts of the experiences that they had gone through with counsellors and therapists. (She uses the two terms interchangeably throughout.) I found these accounts shocking and disturbing to read. It was thoroughly uncomfortable to be confronted with descriptions of members of ‘our’ profession perpetrating acts of sexual abuse with their clients. I found myself inwardly trying to distance and defend ‘my’ orientation (psychoanalytic psychotherapy) from any such accusations. However, Russell does not allow the reader any such easy escape route, suggesting that the sexual exploitation of clients knows no such bounds and crosses the different theoretical schools freely. Such an assertion clearly needs to be backed up in some way, which brings me to a fundamental weakness in the book.

Both in its style and structure, the book has a quasi-social psychology feel to it but lacks any measure of standardised methodology or empirical analysis. Indeed, the number of participants in the research totals only 40 and it is unclear how they came to be selected for inclusion. All the research evidence is thus anecdotal and, while very powerful and emotive, leaves the book vulnerable when it comes to questions of objectivity and rigour. This would have been forgiveable had the author made use of the subjective accounts to further understanding so that clinical practice could be improved, but she has missed a valuable opportunity to do so.

Carlotta Johnson

Carlotta Johnson

Northumberland

Carlotta Johnson  

Humour in psychoanalytic thought and practice is often treated as though it is a kind of defence against and resistance to pain. To avoid sadness and disappointment one turns the situation into a joke. The shifting of attention away from heaviness to lightness is considered unenlightened, unhelpful and destructive to growth and deep development. This can be the case some of the time but humour can also provide an opportunity for movement, integration and insight. It can aid growth and the resolution of conflict.

Laughter, lightheartedness, awareness of the incongruity of a situation can bring into a deadlocked, hopeless, stuck position a kind of energy which is restorative, which lightens things up between two people or among members of a group. The altering of one's view, the taking in of a new perspective, is sometimes easier if it is in the form of a ‘throwaway’ remark. Some psychoanalytic professionals might argue that such kinds of change would not last or be deep enough if accomplished with such fun. It is important to make distinctions in this matter, to know what humour is being used to do: seduce, pevert, obstruct, defend against, deny or to enlarge, enjoy, make freer and so on.

I am arguing this point about humour because I want to have this lighthearted book taken seriously by psychoanalytic psychotherapists. The book was written by a practising psychiatrist who, after many years of working with couples in conflict, decided that most of the literature he had read and on which he had based his therapeutic work was not of much use. Couples got worse and worse through his treatment. This book is the result of his attempts to find ways to enable interpersonal relations to work well. The author considers and emphasises issues which are often overlooked by therapists in treating couples in serious conflict. Some of the rules are: Don't Keep The Romance Alive, Don't Fight Fair, Don't Talk About Everything, Don't Worry About What You Think Is Important. The rules are expanded with short statements. The style of the text is immediate and accessible. Nagler is advocating a comfortable rythym of attachment and separation, encouraging partners to allow room between them. He argues that we live in an overcommunicative age in which we are supposed to talk everything out and resolve everything.

International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, Volume 74, Part 4, 1993

Convergences and Divergences in Contemporary Psychoanalytic Technique

Otto F. Kernberg

A broad survey of the psychoanalytic field reveals both convergences and divergences in technique. The major convergences include earlier interpretation of the transference, increased focus on transference analysis, as well as growing attention to countertransference analysis and increasing concern with the risks of ‘indoctrinating’ patients. Greater emphasis is found on character defences and the unconscious meanings of the ‘here-and-now’. Also noted are trends toward translating unconscious conflicts into object-relations terminology, as well as toward considering a multiplicity of royal roads to the unconscious.

Regarding divergencies, significant controversies continue about the importance of the ‘real’ relationship and the therapeutic versus the resistance aspect of regression. Divergences also continue regarding reconstruction and recovery of preverbal experience, drawing the lines between psychoanalytic psychotherapy and psychoanalysis, the role of empathy, and the relation of historical to narrative truth.



International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, Volume 74, Part 4, 1993

Deficiency and Envy: Some Factors Inpacting the Analytic Mind from Listening to Interpretation

Judith L. Mitrani

This paper examines some aspects of an unconscious process developing within the mind of the analyst; a process affecting both the way in which the analyst listens to the patient's material and the interpretations subsequently formulated. The paper highlights the problem of the analyst's ‘mis-use’ of theory as a protection against unbearable feelings of psychic pain, evoked by what is perhaps the most essential tool of psychoanalysis: the analyst's emotional contact with the patient's early experiences in infancy.

Both the ‘deficiency theory’ and the concept of ‘primary envy’ are called into question during this enquiry. Some of the most recent work of the ‘post’-Kleinians (from Bion through to the present-day workers in England as well as in the Americas) is reviewed. Clinical examples, both from the author's own experience and from previously published material, are considered as illustrative of some factors which may impact upon the mind of the psychoanalyst from listening and interpretation.

Clinical Commentary XVI

[This section is a regular feature. A short piece of clinical material from a session is presented with a brief introduction about the case. The material has been sent ‘blind’ to three people who represent different approachs to the work. They have been asked to comment on the material and the approach. The intention is to put these commentaries on the same material side by side for comparison of the different approaches and to facilitate the understanding of alternative terminologies and modes of practice - Ed]

The Group Facilitator Writes

This is a report of one session of a support group for nurses working on a ward in a large general hospital in the north of England. The group has been meeting weekly for two years, and is attended by the qualified staff nurses and sometimes by other professional staff who work with the ward's patients. It began after one of the nurses approached the Staff Counselling Service for help in facilitating a group to alleviate tension in the staff team. I have been facilitating the group since its inception, and I am a female Staff Counsellor at the same hospital.

The group is held in a small staff room on the ward while the student nurses look after the patients. Usually all the staff nurses on duty at the time attend the group, which is held at a time when the two day-time shifts overlap. When fully staffed the ward employs eleven staff nurses, but due to the shift system each nurse can only attend the group irregularly, and its composition is different each week. There are usually 4-6 group members at each meeting which lasts for fifty minutes.

The ward is a small specialist unit where the emphasis is on rehabilitation but it also takes some general medical or surgical patients. It is well regarded in the hospital and is popular with student nurses. At the time of the group session reported here, the ward had been very short staffed for some months due to a spate of departures of staff nurses. Six had left in the space of three months, including the Senior Staff Nurse who is the deputy of the Charge Nurse.

Klaus Fink

Klaus Fink

London

Klaus Fink  

Mark Aveline has been a psychotherapist for 25 years and has written abundantly about it. This volume is a compilation of some of his thoughts and papers. The book is divided into three parts and 16 chapters. Part I deals with psychotherapy as such, Part II with group psychotherapy and Part III with training and supervision. Dr Aveline offers his ideas and opinions about all these subjects throughout the book and explains in theory and practice how he thinks, how he works and what he believes in. He is an eclectic psychotherapist who draws on all and every school of psychotherapeutic thought; he picks up what suits him best and applies it to his work.

Dr Aveline is the founder and soul of the Psychotherapy Department in Nottingham. In the prologue of his book he gives us a lively account of its beginnings, development and aims. We can see how and why he decides to do something and the result of his decisions. Reading through the book we gain a vivid image of Dr Aveline himself, his work and, most of all, his thoughts and philosophical principles. His left motiv seems to be most of all humanistic although he integrates into it whatever he sees as useful, whether it comes from psychoanalysis (Freudian and Kleinian), from Jung, Rogers, etc., and he seems able to produce a workable result.

Francesca Raphael

Francesca Raphael

London

Francesca Raphael  

The editors' stated aim is to clarify the current theory and practice of art therapy, whilst allowing each of the contributors to express a personal point of view. In fact the thirteen art therapists differ so widely in both theory and practice that I found it hard to discern a single unifying approach that might define art therapy. Notwithstanding this, many of the papers are lively and thought-provoking in their own right.

The early part of the book addresses some of the knotty theoretical issues that continue to divide the profession. The familiar question as to whether art is an intrinsically therapeutic activity or can only be so as part of a therapeutic relationship remains unanswered. Disagreement over such a fundamental philosophical issue goes some way to explain the diversity of opinion and clinical practice evident in the book.

Insecurity about professional status and recognition, a subject which has arisen in much of the art therapy literature (e.g. Dalley & Case 1992, Dalley et al 1987, Waller 1992) is very much in evidence in this publication too. At times it felt a bit repetitive, covering old ground again, and I thought I sensed a somewhat defensive attitude surrounding the whole issue. For example, in attempting to demonstrate the rigour involved in art therapy training, one writer likens it to psychoanalytic training and suggests that art therapists therefore have similar understanding of unconscious processes and motivation. Since art therapy training can be completed in one year and does not yet require that trainees undergo personal therapy or analysis, I felt the comparison was misleading and unconvincing.

As soon as the focus of the book shifts away from art therapy's struggles as a profession to actual descriptions of the work, it becomes far more engaging to read. Each paper contains a review of the literature relevant to its client group, followed by clinical examples. Some papers in particular are worthy of mention.

Christine Wood's account of her work with the chronically mentally ill is beautifully written and shows an uncommon political sensitivity to her client group. She writes with great humility about her work and, in addition, critically evaluates the work of other art therapists in her field. Such public critical discussion is a relatively new, and welcome, phenomenon in the art therapy literature in Britain.

Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy, Volume 7, Number 1, 1993

Psychoanalysis, Psychiatry, Psychodynamics: Training for Integration

Murray Jackson

Despite impressive advances in neurobiology and associated neuro-developmental theory, schizophrenia and related severe mental illnesses continue to follow a chronic or remitting course in the majority of cases.

Psychoanalytic knowledge provides an essential perspective in the attempt to understand and help the severely mentally ill, and such knowledge should not be incompatible with modern findings of neurobiology. The severely ill person is best treated from the outset in a hospital facility where his individual needs and capacities can be fully assessed within an integrated perspective, one which is able to provide a continuing resource as long after discharge as is necessary. A consistent and integrated philosophy of the nature of psychotic illness and its treatment can improve the quality of care provided by psychiatric wards, some of which are both inefficient and anti-therapeutic.

For such a gradual transformation to come about, training of all professional staff in integrating neurobiological and psychoanalytical knowledge is necessary. This paper presents some reflections on the subject deriving from the author's experience in the British National Health Service and in several Scandinavian countries.



Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy, Volume 7, Number 1, 1993

Working with Psychotic Processes in art Therapy

Katherine Killick

In this paper the author describes in some detail her work in the art therapy department of Hill End Hospital. She used not only her understanding of the work of psychoanalytical writers on schizophrenia, particularly Bion and Searles, but, more importantly, her own experience of the patients at the Hospital, to gain an insight into how these very regressed patients think of themselves and their relationship to reality. She illustrates how she used objects and images created by patients from the art materials supplied, during (usually) five two-hour sessions a week, together with conversations (and notes made in the patients' presence of these conversations) about these images at structured weekly individual-therapy sessions, to help patients to develop from a state of meaninglessness to a position in which they can choose to engage in continuing therapy.

Dorothy Rowe

Dorothy Rowe

Sheffield

Dorothy Rowe  

Personal Construct Theory has a long history. The Greek poet Xenophanes wrote in about 500 BC:

The gods did not reveal, from the beginning,

All things to us; but in the course of time,

Through seeking we may learn, and know things better.

But as for certain truth, no man has known it,

Nor will he know it; neither of the gods,

Nor yet of the things of which I speak.

And even if by chance he were to utter

The final truth, he would himself not know it;

For all is but a woven web of guesses.

Four hundred years later Epictetus said ‘It is not things in themselves which trouble us but our opinions of things’. Around the same time one of the authors of the Talmud wrote ‘We see things not as they are but as we are’. In 1725 Giambattista Vico published his New Science where he said ‘Minds are formed by the character of language, not language by the minds of those who speak it’. Later that century Kant, believing that he had revolutionised philosophy, showed that the external world has no absolute being but that we determine it through the mental forms by which we perceive it. From this understanding Ernst Cassirer early this century developed his philosophy concerning the symbolic forms of myth, art, language and science through whose sole agency we can apprehend parts of a reality which lies outside ourselves.

British Journal of Medical Psychology, Volume 66, 43-60, 1993

The Role of Psychological Processes in the Aetiology and Treatment of Cervical Cancer: A Biopsychological Perspective

Peter Lambley

Cervical cancer is one of the most serious illnesses affecting women today, particularly in developing societies. Despite medical advances in treatment and the success of cervical screening programmes in detection, the incidence of the disease is increasing. In this paper it is argued that one of the reasons for this is that the aetiological model employed for cervical cancer takes little account of psychological and psychophysiological factors. Both of these factors are now thought to play important roles in disease processes. Research in these areas is reviewed and a new aetiological model for cervical cancer described. This model incorporates existing epidemiological and medical formulations into a new multifactor framework. The implications of this model for treatment are explored and it is suggested that psychological interventions could play a much greater role than they have in the past.



Journal of Analytical Psychology, Volume 38, Number 3, 1993

‘In a Dark Time, the Eye Begins to See’

Jane Haynes

In this paper I discuss a patient whose shadow became his rival, or as Jung put it, ‘The shadow is lived’. I describe the beginning of a process of the assimilation of shadow contents, whereby the rupture between ego and shadow can no longer be maintained. I also discuss how it is primarily through the mutual experience and analysis of archetypal images that the unconscious contents become more integrated.

In my clinical illustrations I also explore the relationship between my patient's fight with his shadow and his experiences of childhood shame. I consider how fear expressed through a panic attack may open a royal door to the unconscious, and the way in which its mediation through empathy and analysis can lead to unconscious infantile contents becoming more accessible. In addition I show how, once some of the fear had subsided, it became possible for play to enter into the analysis.

Ruth Freeman

Ruth Freeman

Grosvenor Road, Belfast BT12 6BP

Ruth Freeman  

Burning Mouth Syndrome (BMS) is described as a burning sensation of the oral mucosa, tongue, palate, lips and pharynx. The case material presented in this paper illustrates a strong psychogenic element in the aetiology of BMS. Conclusions are drawn on the basis that the patient's material suggests that the recovery of memories played a part in the resolution of her symptoms. The importance this has for psychotherapists is that it allows a reappraisal of the value of using psychoanalytic constructs as a means of understanding the mental representation, symbolisation and psychopathology of conditions of a psychogenic nature.

Response from the BCP

Dear Sir

In Vol. 9 (4), 1993 of the British Journal of Psychotherapy, Mrs Emmy van Deurzen-Smith, Chair of the United Kingdom Council for Psychotherapy described the character of the UKCP and its aims for the future. As the founder institutions of the British Confederation of Psychotherapists, we would like to take the opportunity this gives us to congratulate the UKCP on the impressive achievement which its establishment represents. What may be the eventual benefit of this development to the public, as well as the wide range of its member organisations, should be considerable.

However, since Mrs van Deurzen-Smith also refers in her article to the BCP, we feel it to be essential to respond in order to ensure that the wrong conclusions are not drawn from her remarks.

As the ten founding organisations of the BCP we state in the preamble of the constitution “that the disciplines of psychoanalysis, analytical psychology, psychoanalytic psychotherapy and child psychotherapy comprise the general field of psychoanalytic psychotherapy”. We then state that the public requires “a proper definition of the profession” and that “people will be at risk if they are not able to be sure that practitioners claiming to be psychoanalytic psychotherapists are properly trained and hold membership of a professional association to which they are answerable for their work and for their professional conduct”. Since writing the constitution the BCP has nearly completed a register of organisations and their members who meet the criteria recognised by it as of sufficiently high standard in training and practice to justify membership. So that while Mrs van Deurzen Smith is correct to say that the UKCP and the Confederation are not in a competitive relationship, the truth is not served by her claim that “The (UKCP) is now firmly established as the national umbrella organisation for the entire psychotherapy profession…”

Currently The Association of Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy in the National Health Service, The British Psych-Analytical Society, The Lincoln Centre and Institute for Psychotherapy, The Scottish Association of Psychoanalytical Psychotherapists, The Scottish Institute of Human Relations and The Society of Psycho-Analytical Psychotherapists are members of the Confederation but not of the UKCP.

The British Confederation of Psychotherapists

Update, October 1993

Joscelyn Richards

Joscelyn Richards

Joscelyn Richards  

The Council of the British Confederation of Psychotherapists was inaugurated on 13 September 1993. At this meeting the Shadow Registration and Ethics Committee informed the Shadow Council that they had completed their scrutiny of the training standards and codes of ethics of the participating organisations and recommended that they be approved for membership of the Confederation. This was accepted. The Constitution and the documentation covering training standards, codes of ethics and guidelines for membership had already been voted on at previous meetings.

The following organisations were present and thus constitute the first Council of the Confederation: The Association of Child Psychotherapists, The Association of Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy in the National Health Service, The British Association of Psychotherapists, The British Psycho-Analytical Society, The Lincoln Clinic and Institute for Psychotherapy, The Scottish Association of Psychoanalytical Psychotherapists, The Scottish Institute of Human Relations, The Society of Analytical Psychology, The Society of Psychoanalytical Psychotherapists and The Tavistock Clinic. The newly formed Council voted for five of its members to form the first Executive Committee.

The first task of the Council will be to publish the nearly completed Register of practitioner members of the BCP.

Over the coming months the Executive Committee will negotiate with relevant professional and public bodies to form the proposed Advisory Board whose function it will be to advise the BCP Council in relation to its polices and practices.

External Relations

In June of this year an observer from the BCP attended the Conference held by the Vienna-based European Association for Psychotherapy.

During the Summer, members of the Confederation participated in the Department of Employment's Feasibility Study to see if psychotherapy and counselling have a functional overlap and to see if psychotherapy could be appropriately included within the remit of the Lead Body for Advice, Guidance and Counselling. The BCP members found this to be an unsatisfactory study, partly because of the haste, partly because it did not differentiate between the different forms of psychotherapy and partly because it used a very simple form of functional analysis which does not do justice to the complexity of psychoanalytic psychotherapy. At this stage we think there are major problems with the attempt to fit psychoanalytic psychotherapy into the framework of occupational standards based on functional mapping. Thus we strongly supported the main conclusion of the participants of the Study that a longer, more in-depth investigation was required.

Bristol

Herbert Hahn  

Jeremy Holmes takes us with panache on a wide-ranging celebratory tour and critical evalution of his chosen fields of psychiatry and psychotherapy. Eschewing claims to be an expert, he nevertheless offers us a well-crafted exploration of the fields of dyadic, marital and family psychotherapy, inter alia, through the lens of a psychoanalytically oriented psychiatrist. His approach draws on his understanding of contemporary psychoanalysis and developmental psychology, as well as poetry, literature and the philosophy of science: not to mention Marxism and Zen Buddhism.

The fifteen essays were written over a period of twenty years, with earlier versions of three of them having been published in this journal, and all but two of the rest in related British journals. They are gathered in four parts, the largest of which is a collection of six essays on ‘Analytic Psychotherapy’. The title was probably intended to link with what was the Analytic Psychotherapy Section of the UKSCP, but the contents are in no way diminished by the fact that the section is now called the Psychoanalytic and Psychodynamic Psychotherapy Section, and the UKSCP has become the United Kingdom Council for Psychotherapy. In fact, his final essay entitled ‘Psychotherapy 2000’ not only explores some of the professional dynamics of the UK ‘Analytic Psychotherapy’ scene, but also predicts possible changes in the inter-organisational arena, some of which have since come to pass. His essays in this section endeavour to pose questions or point to a ‘perceived gap’ in psychoanalytic thinking. Clinical illustrations abound, as do clear inferences from selected research and some of the psychoanalytic literature. Not surprisingly, given his own independent, eclectic position (about which he offers a reasoned and balanced exploration), he conveys an impression of an affinity to the ideas of psychoanalysts such as Rycroft, Winnicott, Bollas and Bowlby, while nevertheless exercising the freedom to draw cogently on concepts developed by Klein and Bion, Lacan, Kohut and others. The way in which he seeks his own synthesis is illustrated in a thoroughgoing essay on ‘Obsessional Phenomena’ in which he formulates the view that that a central developmental element in obsessionality is the failure to differentiate reality and phantasy. In addition to clinical examples, his thesis is highlighted by his exploration of the obsession of the protagonist in Proust's Swann's Way, and his concluding remarks include an aside on a possible reason for ‘the success of behaviour therapy in helping the more severe forms of obsessional neurosis’.

Kate Osborne

Kate Osborne  

This detailed account of the influence on Freud's life of significant women - whether his family, patients and colleagues - presents us with a fascinating history of the development of psychoanalysis. The authors, a writer/television producer and a philosopher with a special interest in psychoanalytic ideas, provide a non-partisan view of the life histories their researches describe. After a rather confusing start, where they are confronted with the problem of describing the influence on Freud's early life from material written by people who later became actors in his life's dramas, the book rapidly develops into a remarkable exposé of women's contributions to his work.

We are introduced to the young Freud we are used to knowing, determined to make a name for himself in a scientific career, hampered by lack of finances and constrained to wooing Martha Bernays by lengthy letter-writing where she shows herself to be his intellectual equal. His marriage, and the addition of Martha's sister Minna to his entourage, marked the beginning of his intellectual reliance on women that was to shape the rest of his life. For despite the flamboyant friendships and schisms that marked Freud's relationships with his male associates, notably of course Fliess, Jung and Adler, the exchanges he had with his women confidantes are shown here to hold a pivotal place in the development of his ideas: a place, as so often in the history of women's thinking, that was frequently under-acknowledged.

Peter Lomas  

Why is psychotherapy the focus of so much critical assessment? Religion is similarly the object of debate - indeed, of a very much longer and widespread debate - but it is not haunted and harassed by statistical studies of its efficacy. The reason for the priests' immunity is probably because they do not lay claim to improving things in a way that lends itself to scientific investigation. Perhaps psychotherapists should take note of this.

The criticisms made in Psychotherapy and its Discontents are not of great variety and the theme of statistical proof has a major role in the book. Each essay is followed by a critique from a writer whose interests are appropriate to the task, and the original contributor is given the final word. All the essays, including the elegant preface by Andrew Samuels, are well written - for which the editors deserve our gratitude.

Jeffrey Masson ensures a combative start with a vigorous defence against criticisms of his published work. Masson's passionate attack on hypocrisy in the profession claims our sympathy but his intemperate assault on the personalities of Freud, Jung, Bettelheim and other distinguished psychoanalysts compares unfavourably with the more scholarly and balanced accounts of Paul Roazen. Moreover he fails to consider adequately the bearing of the therapist's personal failings on his or her therapeutic efficacy. If we all had our failings paraded in public few of us would pass muster as models of worthy and sensible behaviour; but this does not, I believe, debar us from practising competent psychotherapy. Masson does, however, have a point. There is, presumably, a threshold of moral frailty beyond which the capacity to help others is seriously diminished. In his sober response to this essay Jeremy Holmes makes some good points but, unfortunately, reveals the very professional complacency that so enrages Masson. And, sure enough, this is exactly what happens again.

When we come to Gellner we leave intemperance behind. Gellner's imaginative excursions into the realm of psychoanalysis are contained by a careful thoughtfulness and are richly rewarding.

Lucy King

Cambridge

Lucy King  

This book comprises a collection of essays written by students on Counselling Diploma courses at Birkbeck College, London. These courses aim to provide a psychodynamic education relevant not just to potential counsellors but also to others whose work ‘has an integral element of responsibility and concern for the emotional health and development of people’.

A couple of chapters are straightforward case histories but most are based on the

368

dissertations which each student writes at the end of the two-year course. In these the task was to relate the theory learned in the classroom to issues arising in the context of their work, be it as counsellor, teacher, youth worker or whatever. Thus not all the chapters are directly concerned with counselling but all try to show how psychodynamic thinking can deepen one's understanding of the people with whom one works.

I appreciate the desire behind the publication of these essays. Considerable thought and experience go into such dissertations and the results often merit a wider audience than the course examiners. Reading the volume, however, it is clear that it both gains and suffers from having its origins in student assignments. The theoretical base drawn upon is sometimes rather restricted, conveying the impression that the authors have all read the same books and/or attended the same seminars.

On the other hand, perhaps even as a consequence of their relative lack of theoretical sophistication, the papers are written with a freshness, clarity and directness which makes them interesting and accessible to a non-specialist or student readership. There is none of the condescension or chummy joviality that sometimes mars popularising accounts of psychological themes.

Another merit of the book's scope and format is that it gives a sense of the breadth of settings in which counselling skills are put to use. The range of both settings and clientele makes salutary reading for psychotherapists who tend to look down on mere counselling. The therapeutic aims of much of this work may be limited but the tasks faced by some of these counsellors are challenging in the extreme. In fact, in some ways it is the therapist in his or her counselling room who could be judged to have the easier, more straightforward job. For here we have accounts of struggles to keep appropriate therapeutic boundaries without the supportive structures of setting and schedules most of us can take for granted. Counsellors working in the field; in clients' homes or in youth clubs; counsellors with dual roles of counsellor and adviser; counsellors working in agencies with multiple roles; counsellors working with clients most therapists either would not encounter or would not choose to work with.

Journal of Analytical Psychology, Volume 37, Number 4, 1992

Some Functions of the Self Personified by the Father

Richard Carvalho

I have presented clinical material in order to illustrate a series of fantasies of parental intercourse which represent the self in successive stages of individuation from early projective identification to later introjective identification. From this is abstracted the idea of ‘father’ both as a component of the self representation and as the personification of the urge towards continuing development. Evidence is also gathered from the clinical material, supported by mythological parallels, to suggest that the whole process, including those components explicitly identified with the mother, is subsumed under an identification of the deintegrating self, its identity and integrity, with ‘the father’.



Journal of Analytical Psychology, Volume 37, Number 4, 1992

Marion Milner's Pre-Freudian Writings, 1926-1938: The Originality and Origins of Her Creativity Model

Paul Watsky

Marion Milner's writings c. 1926-1938, comprising the books A Life of One's Own, An Experiment in Leisure and The Human Problem in Schools, are discussed. The author speculates that Marion Milner's work has received little scholarly attention in the psychoanalytic world because it is difficult to contain within traditional theoretical categories. Her professional background and temperament dispose Marion Milner to wide-ranging interests and a practical approach to psychological issues. This article explores parallels between her ideas and Jungian thought, especially the contribution of unconscious process to organizing creative activity in a more coherent fashion than is attributed to primary process thinking. The author concludes that Marion Milner has developed an efficient model of creative process, consisting of the cyclical bimodal alternation of introverted and extraverted energy, mediated by symbolic imagery and the artist's interaction with the medium.

Editorial

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood  

Is it not interesting that in 1899 Hungary had a Journal devoted to therapy? The histories of psychotherapy and psycho-analysis in Britain and Hungary are widely different, due of course to the vastly differing social and political histories. Such cultural divergence led no doubt to the emergence of the towering originality of Sandor Ferenczi in Hungary, whilst in Britain Ernest Jones dedicated himself more to the pragmatic role of organising the psycho-analytic movement. One cannot perhaps judge whose was the greater contribution, only to note the major contrast in their types of achievement.

Ferenczi's birthday, 120 years ago is being celebrated this July in Budapest with an International Conference. But it surely also celebrates the emergence of the enormously renewed interest in psycho-analysis in Eastern Europe. And we publish a clutch of papers (gathered by Martin Stanton) in this issue of the Journal; including an obituary by Ferenczi of a man who was an important early influence on him.

Contemporary with the rehabilitation of psycho-analysis in Eastern Europe, the psycho-analytic world in general is beginning a rehabilitation of Ferenczi - see for instance Andre Haynal (1988) The Technique at Issue: Controversies in Psycho-Analysis from Freud and Ferenczi to Michael Balint (London: Karnac); Martin Stanton (1991) Sandor Ferenczi: Reconsidering Active Intervention (London: Free Association Books); Sandor Ferenczi (1990) Clinical Diaries (Cambridge, Mass: Harvard University Press).

Ernest Jones, Melanie Klein and Michael Balint were Ferenczi's foremost analysands in Britin. Jones and Klein went their own ways but Balint brought his own special commitment to Ferenczi. Despite that he created only a moderate respect for Ferenczi himself. This no doubt goes back to the early thirties when Ferenczi and Jones were in intense rivalry for Freud's favour (Ferenczi to hang on to it, and Jones to take it over); and eventually Jones succeeding in achieving the position of President of The International Psycho-Analytical Association in place of Ferenczi. But these rivalries, once embedded in the cultural folk-law, persist for a very long time to keep groups and cultures distinct from each other. This exclusion of Ferenczi is now breaking down, particularly with a renewed examination of his proposals for modifications in technique.

What does ‘facilitating a support group’ mean? A lot of such work goes on. The answer is never clear. I assume that, as the support group is an institutional resource timetabled in work time for optimal involvement of nurses on different shifts, the task is about supporting staff to be effective in their work. It is not a therapy group although the facilitator is also a counsellor in the hospital. All we can do as group facilitator is examine our relationship to the institution when we take up such a role and learn about the nature of the institution and the experience of some of the people working in it.

Ordinary Miseries: Extraordinary Remedies

Liam Clarke

Liam Clarke

Falmer, Brighton BN1 9RT

Liam Clarke  

Joel Kovel (1978) refers to rational emotive therapy as part of a post-analytic group of therapies and, in particular, as part of the modern ‘human potential movement’ that has evolved since the nineteen fifties. In fact, Rational Emotive Therapy (RET) was the brainchild of Albert Ellis, produced as part of a theory of personality and research in clinical psychology. Whilst ostensibly part of the ‘human potential movement’ it is here (parsimoniously) assigned to the more narcissistic elements within that movement but becoming more abrasive as the overall political culture in Britain and America changed from the mid-seventies.

The importance of the cultural setting for this particular approach becomes obvious when one considers the values and assumptions upon which it is based; a rational world of individualism and essentially pragmatic selfhood where outcomes are viewed as a consequence of distorted beliefs and where personal interpretations determine future events and mould the course of our lives. In general, the cultural milieu within which therapies work has been a neglected issue resulting in the emergence of a profession which is largely unexamined - other than by therapists themselves - as well as largely unaccounted for.

Freudian Loss

Much of the meaning of the work of Sigmund Freud had become lost in translation, for instance, a position recently summarised by the late Bruno Bettelheim. Analysis, according to a German reading of Freud, was a softer and more compassionate therapy than in the hands of the Americans who, more than any others, turned it into a dispassionate (medically dominated) system of abstractions, avoiding personal feelings between therapist and patient preferring instead, ‘A way of looking only at others, from a safe distance’ (Bettelheim 1983, p. 6). Freud had assumed a cultured audience for his books and papers: according to Bettelheim (1983) he thought that Americans lacked the kind of classical learning (stories of the Gods and their naughty offspring) possessed by educated Europeans. The assumption here is that psychoanalysis springs from a deep well: that it comes from a long and thickly planted European culture (quite apart from the European tendency to assume easy sociological constructs on a monumental scale: ‘dark continents’, ‘third worlds’ and the like): that the notion of psychoanalysis is about coming to know oneself in a profound way, in a way which would be profound and moving enough to warrant the company of Gods.

The Field of Psychotherapy: Conceptual and Ethical Definitions

Karl Figlio

Karl Figlio

24 Roseberry Avenue, Colchester COI 2UJ

Karl Figlio  

In this paper* I hope to show that the conceptual structure of psychotherapy (I will consider only psychoanalytical psychotherapy) has an ethical character: that is, it contains assessments of valued and devalued aspects of human psychology. I will add to this argument the assumption that a professional field builds its identity substantially around a specialised body of knowledge and organised inquiry. It follows that its ethical character informs its structure and identity, not just through sanctions, but through knowledge, research and teaching - through the way it reproduces itself.

In the 1960s and 1970s - certainly since Thomas Kuhn's The Structure of Scientific Revolutions in 1962- a paper on the relationship between the conceptual repertoire and the ethical character of a scientific field - broadly, a paper on the social character of scientific knowledge - would have found its place within an ongoing lively debate. (There is a substantial literature in this area which lies outside the main concern of this paper. I will cite only two references, which give a flavour of the issues of the time and include extensive bibliographies: Figlio 1977; Wright & Treacher 1982.) Times have changed; the political climate has changed: the recent debates on cosmogeny, artificial human reproduction and religion, for example, have been polarised and inflamed. But the moral evaluation of all that we do, whether in the form of assigning responsibility for the environmental impact of technological progress or of concern about research into human fertilisation, has nonetheless diffused into culture. There is a sense that scientific inquiry should be included within public discussion: that valuing should be part of knowing; that an interest in the nature of society should have at least equal footing with the appreciation of what that society produces, including its science.

Psychotherapy in Britain, and in Europe as a whole, is at a critical juncture: the pressures in the European Community (and the European Free Trade Association) to create a structure for a profession have brought to the surface the schismatic and hegemonic forces that had hitherto remained latent in the UK. They have promoted the formation of the United Kingdom Standing Conference for Psychotherapy and, at the European level, have produced the European Association for Psychotherapy and the European Federation for Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy in the Public Sector. As the momentum towards professional organisation picks up, so do the claims of various bodies to speak for the profession, to liaise with government, to set training criteria, to monitor training programmes, and to assess and register graduates.

Charles Rycroft

London

Charles Rycroft  

The name if not the person of Nina Coltart will be familiar to many readers of this journal. As the blurb correctly says, she is a distinguished member of the Independent Group within the British Psychoanalytical Society, who has at various times been Vice-President of the Society and Director of the London Clinic of Psychoanalysis. She is also well known as a speaker, a supervisor, a source of referrals not only from the London Clinic but also from her private consulting practice, and for her encouragement of psychotherapy training centres, notably the Arbours Association. Slouching Towards Bethelehem is, we are told, her first collection of writings, the implication being that there will be more to come.

As the Independent Group is not a formal school of psycho-analysis but rather a collection of, hopefully, independent-minded eclectic analysts, Dr Coltart's position within it demands further definition. The analysts of the preceding generation who seem to have influenced her most are Winnicott, Bion, Balint and Laing; the contemporary analysts she quotes most often are Christopher Bollas and Neville Symington. Rather surprisingly, in view of the fact that she is insistent that psychoanalysis is a moral not a natural science and that religion is not just a neurotic's illusion, she is at pains to emphasise her indebtedness to Sigmund Freud; she appears to have a particular affection for the tripartite, structural conception of the personality that he developed in the 1920s, but it is noticeable that she eschews the phrase ‘psychic apparatus’, and, I gather, conceives of the tripartite, psychic structure as a convenient metaphor and not as an explanatory hypothesis.

However, Dr Coltart is not, and would not, I think, claim to be, a theoretician. The papers included in Slouching Towards Bethlehem are not scientific contributions to the psychopathology of specific neuroses but, rather, meditations on what sort of an activity psychoanalysing is, on what attitude an analyst should take up to his (her) profession and patients and, more personally, to what extent her own way of doing things differs from standard, conventional practice.

Freud himself was dubious about the possibilities for psychoanalysis in Italy and its current position is comparatively recent. Twenty-one years of fascism had not provided a suitable climate for its growth and by the end of 1938 almost all the remaining analysts of a group which had always been small had gone abroad. Even before that its reception had been critical, especially in the faculties of medicine and psychology. This related partly to the dominance of the socio-anthropological positivism which was the inheritance of Lombroso and partly to Catholicism in general and its links to psychology in particular. Other political and intellectual components of Italian culture, Crocean idealism and Marxism (especially later) were also unenthusiastic. Souls in Armour: Thoughts on Psychoanalysis and Racism**

Paul Gordon

Paul Gordon

16 Kenilworth Road, London NW6 7HJ

Paul Gordon  

For A Sivanandan, it miglior fabbro, from whom I have learned

Introduction

I tell you, they have our souls in armour. (Black woman quoted in Cottle 1978)

What is at issue is the apparent incapacity to constitute oneself as oneself without excluding the other, coupled with the apparent inability to exclude the other without devaluing and, ultimately, hating them. (Castoriadis 1992)

Addressing the question of psychoanalysis and racism, I do so necessarily as a split subject. On the one hand, I am a public citizen, abhorring the injustice of racism and the brutalities done in its name. On the other, I am also a psychotherapist trying, to borrow Spinoza's words, neither to laugh nor to weep but to understand, trying too to bear in mind Freud's distinction between thought and feeling on the one hand and action and behaviour on the other. ‘On the couch, neurosis,’ Freud once remarked, ‘In real life, swinish behaviour’.

Someone more theatrical than myself might well dramatise this split, leaping from one side of the table to the other as the parts switch or speaking in different voices. But I shall spare myself-and you-the spectacle of even attempting this.

When I agreed to give this lecture I had the grandiose idea that I would be able to do what my sub-title implies, that is if not lay down a psychoanalytic theory, then at least be moving close to it. I feel I must come clean at the outset and state that my reading and thoughts have taken me somewhere else, for reasons which I hope I shall make clear to you.

What I want to present to you are some thoughts on the relationship between racism and psychoanalysis-to look at what psychoanalysis has had to say-and more important not say-about racism and to explore the tension between a political understanding of racism and a psychological, in particular, a psychoanalytic one. I want to offer some thoughts too about more useful ways of looking at this subject.

What I have to say very much represents work in progress, a contribution to a conversation I believe to be important. Some lines from T S Eliot's East Coker seem appropriate in this context: ‘… a raid on the inarticulate/With shabby equipment always deteriorating/In the general mess of imprecision of feeling,/Undisciplined squads of emotion’.

Why Analysts Need Their Patients' Transferences

Charles Rycroft

Charles Rycroft

2 Modbury Gardens, London NW5 3QE.

Charles Rycroft  

This paper is an addendum to, and in some ways a correction of, an earlier paper of mine (Rycroft 1985) in which I suggested that some people aspire, sometimes successfully, to become psycho-analysts in order to deny the psychical reality of their actual parents and to replace them by surrogate parents of their own choosing. Such people, I argued, ablate the images of their parents and replace them by those of their training analyst and supervisors, and trace their ancestry not from their actual forebears but from the dynasty founded by Freud when he created the psychoanalytical movement.

In this present paper I shall suggest that some analysts succeed in retaining or recovering their infantile sense of omnipotence by means of projective identification; that they attribute to, project onto, their training analyst (or, if he or she is hopelessly uncharismatic, some other revered analyst) their own infantile sense of omnipotence, identify with this idealised recipient of their own projections, and thereby recapture, re-introject, their infantile sense of omnipotence.

In arguing this idea I shall start not from Melanie Klein's and Herbert Rosenfeld's writings on projective identification but from the paper in which, according to Rosenfeld, the concept of projective identification first appears in the psychoanalytical literature.* This is Otto Fenichel's Trophy and Triumph, which was first published in German in 1939 and in English in the Second Series of his Collected Papers (Fenichel 1955).

In the first section of this paper Fenichel observes that children retain a belief in omnipotence long after the loss of their own sense of it and do so by regarding as omnipotent their parents, the very persons who have so seriously limited their own. In other words, the infant's illusion of his own omnipotence is followed by, replaced by, the illusion of parental omnipotence. Fenichel then goes on to say that this leads to an attempt by the child to seize power from the omnipotent parent, to eliminate him or to rob him of his power. But ‘if this cannot be achieved, another means is adopted. The individual allows the powerful being to remain, but in some way partakes of his power - (he) re-introjects the power he has projected’.

Response to Anthony Ryle

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

16a Glyn Mansions, Avonmore Road, London W14 8XH

Ann Scott  

My starting point in responding to Anthony Ryle's provocative critique of Betty Joseph's ‘Addiction to near-death’ is Dr Ryle's closing comment: ‘one year in analysis uses enough professional time to treat ten patients in this category with CognitiveAnalytic Therapy’. A debate in this area is particularly welcome because it brings together two widespread concerns: one theoretical, one about resources; I should like to suggest a third term for discussion, absent from Ryle's paper: the lastingness of psychic change. For it seems to me that this is a pivot around which to explore questions about resources and treatments of choice.

But first, some comments about Dr Ryle's presentation of Joseph. It is true that the reader has to take quite a lot on trust. Betty Joseph's patient is a theorised patient. And, in my view, Dr Ryle is right to ask the question that one would ask of any clinical approach: what mobilises the patient's capacities? It is also a bullseye to speak of hyperbole in the presentation of the patient's psychic life. But there are some unresolved theoretical issues, too. Ryle tells us what has been discarded from object relations but not what has been retained (I wish he had); and CAT's theorisation of a division of the human personality would have been helped by an unpacking of the steps by which the (to my mind) rather functionalist, benign account of role procedures gives way to a more nuanced picture of a self at odds with itself. And I hope I am not caricaturing CAT in concluding that psychic damage comes primarily ‘from outside’ (the stress on adverse circumstances). So we have a view of human relationships in which even severe disturbances of mental functioning can be modified by the provision of a task-oriented therapeutic setting in which the therapist and patient agree on a new, shared language and set of procedures that will initiate and reinforce change.

At its heart, however, Joseph's paper is concerned with the question of refusal: the refusal of psychic change, and not just at a surface operational level. In terms of the deep structures of the mind: the tenaciousness of isolating, hurtful and self-destructive dispositions and acts. In Joseph's terms such dispositions and acts would, I think, constitute manifestations of the death instinct. On what basis might we accept this account of the mind? CAT, as Ryle says, does not. I do not think such a basic disagreement can be bridged.

Meira Likierman

Meira Likierman

5 Downshire Hill, London NW3 INK

Meira Likierman  

No one wrote an introduction to Sandor Ferenczi's works for over half a century after his death. In some respects Ferenczi has been the eccentric relative in the family of psychoanalysis who was to be left muttering harmlessly in the corner and not properly introduced. For he was somewhat embarrassing. He advocated worrying practices such as ‘mutual analysis’ and ‘active technique’ (Ferenczi 1920). And as if these irresponsible sounding methods do not arouse enough suspicion, there were rumours of a psychotic breakdown late in his life as well as allegations that he was promisouous with patients. Perhaps this reputation partly accounts for the fact that, in spite of Ferenczi's position as founding member and some time President of the International Psycho-analytical Association, there has been relatively little critical appreciation of his importance (Stanton 1990).

In spite of a growing interest in Ferenczi's thinking a caution towards him lingers in academic psychoanalytic circles. His techniques have been defined as ‘highly controversial’ (Greenberg & Mitchell 1985) and his contribution to psychoanalysis typically summed up in terms of his followers more than himself: ‘as the analyst of Klein, Balint and Clara Thompson, Ferenczi was an important figure, directly or indirectly, in the psychoanalytic lineage of all the major relational model innovators’ (Greenberg & Mitchell 1985). There has been broad consensus on such views. Ferenczi has been valued more as an ‘influence’ than a thinker in his own right. Perhaps for this reason his works have traditionally barely figured on the reading lists of Kleinian theory courses in Britain.

Yet a direct approach to Ferenczi's texts cannot fail to enrich as well as challenge. Ferenczi rarely recycles psychoanalytic givens without simultaneously being inspired to fresh insights and additions. Whether these seem brilliant or implausible, they reveal a startling originality and an extraordinary intuitive resource. His is a deeply creative imagination that proliferates with everything from the exquisite and rare to the wild and eccentric. In our rush to weed out the latter we should take care not to trample over the former.

[[RunningHead]]

Prejudice

Bernard Ratigan

Bernard Ratigan

Bernard Ratigan  

Dear Sir

Dr Denman (‘Prejudice and Homosexuality’, BJP Vol 9 No 3) takes me to task, amongst other things, for being prejudiced. Many of her points are well argued. With the benefit of hindsight I wish now I had written that ‘some’ rather than ‘many of those who had acquired the virus…’ etc. Over-generalization is one of the besetting sins of the clinicians attempting to write about their work. The talk on which the article was based was first given in 1989. My current views on psychoanalytic psychotherapy in the treatment of people with borderline or narcissistic personality disorders affected by HIV were presented at the 1993 Berlin World AIDS Conference (Ratigan 1993a).

As an out gay psychoanalytic psychotherapist running an HIV service in a department of genito-urinary medicine, I see patients either for consultation or treatment, who all have major mental health problems, most of which predate their testing positive and usually have their roots in infancy or childhood, otherwise they would be seeing a counsellor or health adviser. By far the majority of the HIV patients I treat are gay men, reflecting the epidemiology of the condition in England and Wales. Many have chosen or asked to see or been referred by consultant physicians to another gay man for therapy. I do also see numbers of heterosexual men and women only a minority of whom are drug users. I am unaware of clear psychopathologies that can be attributed to patient category. What I do think though is that we all seek in sexual union, amongst other things, the resolution or repetition of the early infant/mother relationship. This puts us all at risk as the virus is no respecter of so called ‘risk categories’ and especially those who have the most vulnerable psychic cores. Reading Dr Denman I began to wonder if I had been imagining the severity of the disturbances of the patients I see in my HIV clinic.

I do not think we serve our patients, profession or truth by pretending that, for whatever reason, there are not quite a few people in the gay community with serious mental health problems (see, for example, Catalan et al 1992). Surely, as a community we are now moving to a position where we can be open about the problems some of us face as a way of beginning to explore why this is so and what can be done about it. A start has been made by initiatives such as the symposium on issues in gay male sexual identity at the March 1993 annual conference of the British Psychological Society (Ratigan 1993b). The vicissitudes which those of us who put this symposium together attest to the institutional homophobia which needs exposing and remedying. We should also be grateful to Dr Denman for her paper as it allows this important debate to take place in the fresh-air of the intellectual market place rather than in the ghetto.

When I first broached the idea of a conference about ‘psychoanalysis and ecology’ it was met with enthusiasm tempered with a certain amount of incredulity from my colleagues. What has psychoanalysis - dealing above all with the subtle nuances of an intersubjective communication between patient and therapist - have to say about this global issue concerned with the physical environment? Such misgivings echoed a recurring argument about the proper domain of psychoanalysis as both a theory and therapy.

The problem (of the relation between psychoanalysis and cultural issues) is often couched in terms of the difference between the ‘individual’ and the ‘social’ as separate fields of enquiry. Even without resorting to the theories of group analysis or the psychoanalysis of institutions, this may not in fact be the case. Psychotherapy deals with the ‘social’ all the time in its strictly private and individual setting. Concerned as it is with the minutiae of an individual's life, psychotherapy in practice also involves something of the behaviour we engage in as a (unique, cultural) species. It is this behaviour which generates the ecological dilemmas which confront us, and about which psychoanalysis should have something to say.

According to Freud there are certain universals of what we might call ‘human nature’ which are expressed in our cultural productions. All cultures will have to find some way to negotiate the problems caused by the combination of our childhood dependence and infantile sexuality which results in the Oedipus complex; all cultures will have to find some ‘social’ mechanisms whereby primitive anxieties are dealt with; all societies must find some way to deal with the anxieties associated with procreative sexuality; and all societies will have means to regulate the impact of ‘other people’ on our essentially narcissistic economy,* and so on. Mary Heller

Mary Heller

Woodlands Road Clinic, Middlesbrough, Cleveland TS1 3BL

Mary Heller  

In this paper I explore the case of a woman, Miss M, whose twin died ‘in embryo’, employing as an extended metaphor Coleridge's Rime of the Ancient Mariner. Both the poem and Miss M's story describe ‘internal world’ dramas formed through very early object relationships. In Coleridge's allegorical poem we are told much about the poet's own inner world. The poem contains universal themes of destructiveness, loss and the quest for reparation; these themes illuminate the patient's story which was recounted by Miss M during assessment sessions for psychotherapy. The impact of her story, particularly its maritime images, formed many associative connections in my mind with the poem. The result for me was an enriched understanding of both the patient and the poem.

[[RunningHead]]

Psychological Processes of Consuming

Susie Orbach

Susie Orbach

2 Lancaster Drive, London NW3 4HA

Susie Orbach  

Consumerism has defined a whole culture's relationship to itself over the last two decades (Williamson 1986, Orbach 1986). The way we enter and partake of the public sphere is not through the exercise of conventional political relationships but through the relations of consumption. To be excluded from the relations of consumption is to be disenfranchised.

At the turn of the century, the development of the department store (and mail order through Sears Roebuck) in the United States had the effect of enfranchising women across the class spectrum. Similar products on sale on different floors with different price tags allowed working-class women to emulate middle-class values and so join in the dominant culture. Immigrant women, seeking to assimilate, battled with parental values of the old country to wear the clothes of the New World thus allowing them participation in the American Dream (Ewan & Ewan 1982).

In the UK and Western Europe, consumerism is a very recent post World War Two development, not really taking off seriously until the long economic boom of the 60's when fashion, hi-fi's, cars and other consumer durables became available at a mass level. In the 1980's we saw politicians exhorting the righteousness of consuming. Both the left and the right introduced the concept of the citizen as consumer. In an ironic twist from the prevailing pre-consumerist puritanism where ascetism was prized - especially for the needy - and consuming was reserved as the privileged activity of the wealthy, conservative politicians hopped on the bandwagon of consumerism as a way to deal with the difficulties inherent in present political programmes.

Along with consumerism went movements which, while not essentially anticonsumerist, contained within them an implicit critique of consumerism. First the Beats, then the hippies and the New Left rejected the conformity and the encoded statuses associated with consumerism. The Greens were the first explicitly anticonsumerist movement but consumerism has now become so highly complex that one can even consume in politically correct ways.

These two volumes represent the best and most up-to-date accounts of Langs' work. In spite of this, there is little if any overlap between the two books which supplement one another. In my opinion they are both extremely important contributions to psychoanalytic theory.

A Clinical Workbook for Psychotherapists is a one-volume edition of a three-volume set first published by Newconcept Press in 1985. This book is a comprehensive statement of Langs' theory of technique using a highly innovative format. Brief theoretical discussions are interspersed with learning exercises, enabling the reader to acquire the basic cognitive skills required for communicative psychoanalytic work. Typically, a theoretical concept is introduced, which is then followed by a clinical vignette and a series of questions inviting the reader to apply the theoretical concept to the clinical material. Langs then provides answers which the reader can compare with his or her own. This approach may seem strange to many psychoanalytic practitioners but it flows naturally from Langs' theory which, as the book shows, is a highly systematic and rigorous approach to formulating unconscious meaning and intervening. The book goes several steps beyond such texts, as, for example, Greenson's Technique and Practice of Psycho-Analysis, which use vignettes for illustrative purposes without explicitly inviting the reader to engage with the clinical material.

The Role of Psychoanalytic Studies in Psychotherapy Training

Martin Stanton

Martin Stanton

24-31 The Market, London SE10 9HZ

Martin Stanton  

The future direction of psychotherapy training and research in this country will be determined to a great extent by the relationship between training bodies, which are mostly in the private sector, and the universities, the vast majority of which operate in the public sector. There are compelling reasons why universities will be the prime movers in determining the nature of this relationship, and indeed prime movers in determining the nature of psychotherapy as an academic subject: government funds will increasingly become available to grant-assist university trainings; government grant-assisted institutions are subsequently more likely to receive work from other government institutions such as the health service, social services and education; from the trainee's point of view, the overall costs of training, including personal therapy and supervision costs, will be grant-assisted in university psychotherapy courses, thus making them more attractive propositions than private sector trainings. Even if government policy changed, and a North American-style student loan system was introduced, universities would still be state subsidised, and more likely to attract outside funding than the private sector trainings. This logic obviously explains both the attractiveness and seeming inevitability of university validation for trainings in the private sector.

This logic is not isolated to psychotherapy and does indeed exist in other clinically related subjects, such as psychology and medicine. It also exists in psychotherapy trainings in other European countries, such as Germany and Holland, albeit within the strict academic boundaries of psychology and medicine. Unfortunately, in Britain, there are major differences in the ways that private-sector psychotherapy training bodies and universities operate; differences which, if left unaddressed, may well seriously hinder both the academic and professional development of psychotherapy. First of all, there are the obvious differences between the ‘standards’ of clinical work, which have been so ardently disputed amongst psychotherapy trainings in recent months, and the ‘standards’ of academic work. Crucial here is the academic notion of scholarship, which not only implies a special place for rigorous research and debate of different positions, but also implies particular methods of examination and assessment, such as double or triple marking of essays and the obligatory supervision of an external examiner. Most, if not all the British psychotherapy, psychoanalytic and analytical psychology trainings would presently be unable to meet such requirements as far as the written components of their courses are concerned.

January 1993: Chairman's Opening Address

Michael Pokorny

Michael Pokorny

Michael Pokorny  

It is with great pleasure and some sadness that I open the annual conference from the Chair for the last time. On Sunday morning my four years as your chairman will be over and a new chairperson will be elected. I am proud of our achievements together and look forward to our future as the Profession of Psychotherapy. I am very pleased that I will still have a part to play in the immediate future, as I have been appointed by Council to be the first Chair of the Registration Board.

Before I tell you how much we must do this weekend let me very quickly remind you of just how far we have travelled together since those far-off days of the Rugby Psychotherapy Conference.

After the Foster Report of 1971 and the collapse of the Professions Joint Working Party in 1978 came the Private Members Bill to regulate psychotherapy, which failed in 1981. That Bill was moved by Graham Bright MP who is still keeping in close touch with us and advising and helping us. In 1982 the British Association for Counselling invited organisations to the first of what was to develop into the Rugby Psychotherapy Conferences. Run on a shoestring those Rugby Conferences laid the groundwork for the Standing Conference which was inaugurated in 1989. Of course, by then we had outgrown Rugby and had settled here in Canterbury. In 1989 we had sixty-six organisations in membership. Since then we have grown to seventy organisations in spite of refusing entry to about forty and losing six. We expelled one last year and five left of their own accord.

At the Inaugural Meeting in January 1989 I recall saying to you that I wished that I had a shilling for every time somebody had said to me: ‘You will never get that lot to agree to anything’. In fact we have reached agreement on a wide variety of important matters. Since inauguration we have all worked very hard to get to the stage of agreeing the structures that we need to create and administer a Register of Psychotherapists and we will be putting those in place this weekend. We have agreed on the foundations of a common basis of minimum acceptable training standards and have made useful contacts with the Department of Health and the Department of Trade. We have attended a meeting of European Co-Ordinators in Brussels and are now in the position that no initiative on psychotherapy can be made within the structures of the European Community without our being notified. We have also made contact with a Member of the European Parliament and begun what I am sure will be a long and fruitful liaison with her.

Measurements of change in family functioning during admission to the In-Patient Families Unit at the Cassel Hospital were devised, defined, and used to compare 14 families who were seen to make beneficial changes in their functioning as a result of in-patient treatment with 14 families who were not seen to make such a change during admission. [[RunningHead]]

Introduction

Martin Stanton

Martin Stanton

Martin Stanton  

Richard Sterba in his Reminiscences of a Viennese Psychoanalyst (1982) recalls humorously a lecture that Ferenczi gave in Berlin in the 1920s, during which he advocated that analysts should see only one or two patients a day. This went right against the trend in Berlin where analysts were increasingly encouraged to see more and more patients, so there was considerable lively controversy at question time. After the lecture a group took Ferenczi to a popular night-club, where Josephine Baker was to perform her celebrated ‘exotic dance’. Much to the surprise of the analysts, after losing many of her clothes, Ms Baker danced her way through the packed room towards their table where she proceeded to sit herself on Ferenczi's knee and, much to his glee, affectionately rubbed his bald head! Sterba viewed this incident as illustrative both of Ferenczi's unique personal charisma and the total impossibility of ever generalising his ‘new’ technique: the only person who could ever be an analyst in the Ferenczian mould was Ferenczi himself!

This view has proved remarkably resilient as there is still as much biographical fascination with Ferenczi as there is interest in his ideas. The publication of his Clinical Diary in 1989, and the forthcoming publication of the first volume of his correspondence with Freud, have only further fuelled this fascination - though as much to Ferenczi's detriment as to his aggrandisement: the Diary has re-opened old controversies about his expriments in ‘mutual analysis’, that is, allowing the patient to act as analyst in certain circumstances (which Freud dubbed the ‘kissing technique’), and the Letters are sure to fuel dispute about both Freud and Ferenczi's total lack of confidentiality and manipulative use of analysis to resolve their personal problems (notably in the case of Ferenczi's affair with Elma Palos - his patient and daughter of his lover).

Nonetheless, Ferenczi's innovations have recently become extremely topical, not least because of his unique work on the effects of sexual abuse of children. Ferenczi also ardently advocated that analysis should ‘democratise’ itself, that is adjust itself to meet the demands of ordinary people: it should be state-subsidised or free if possible, and should develop brief or ‘focal’ methods to treat major neurotic disorders. Furthermore, analysis should develop its own methods of training and break free of the medical model; post-graduation, all analysts should also have permanent supervision to contain the negative effects of countertransference. At the time of his death in 1933, all these issues ultimately isolated him from all but a few of the psychoanalytic community. Sixty years later, they have transformed him into a prime source of study of the early development of the main concerns of contemporary psychoanalysis. He is increasing seen as an analyst years ahead of his time, and as an early and fearless explorer of the ‘unhappy consciousness’ of the psychoanalytic profession.

Comment on Ferenczi and Schachter

Judit Meszaros PHD

Judit Meszaros

Budapest

Judit Meszaros  

Who would have believed that a surgeon could contribute to the development of Hungarian psychoanalysis? Are there any fields within medical science so remote from each other as surgery and psychology?

In his obituary to Miksa Schachter (Ferenczi 1917), which contained many autobiographical remarks, Sandor Ferenczi - famous Hungarian psychoanalyst, one of the closest associates of Freud - says farewell to the editor-in-chief of Gyogyaszat. Who was this man who had such a great influence on young Ferenczi, and to whom he addressed the following words (Ferenczi 1917):

I felt that his personality could be compared to a single piece of perfect marble free of fractures or fault … It was truly a period which shaped my character.

Five years after finishing his medical studies, Miksa (Maximilian) Schachter became the owner and editor-in-chief of Gyogyaszat at the age of 27 in 1886. At that time the Hungarian medical community had two medical journals: Orvosi Hetilap (Medical Weekly) for the leading circles and well-known for its conservative attitude; and Gyogyaszat, representing an opposing position, founded by an editor quitting the former's editorial board in 1861. Gyogyaszat was intended to be a forum of ‘the progress of Hungarian and international medicine, especially that of medical practice’. The journal edited by Schachter resembled the British Medical Journal. Main topics were always introduced by editorials; not only medical papers and book reviews, but also writings covering the problems of medical public life were published.

Schachter was just over thirty when he started work as a clerk in the newly-founded Council of Forensic Medicine and devoted his life to fighting against unethical medical practices. People were struck by Schachter's deeply humanistic thinking, openmindedness and courageous stand in matters he believed true. Schachter's parents wanted him to become a Rabbi and he was educated accordingly. He spoke Hebrew, had substantial knowledge of Judaism and possessed excellent knowledge of German, French and English. Schachter knew English literature well; his papers contained many biblical references and quotations from Shakespeare. Schachter's principal aim was to seek the common points of various phenomena. Neither was he prejudiced against views differing from his own. A typical example of Schachter's approach: in the same year (1899) that Ferenczi's article on spiritualism was published (Ferenczi 1899), Schachter wrote on reasons that might lead to the formation of a variety of sects in medicine. Homeopathy is Schachter's other example to demonstrate that mutual demarcation rather than employing the principle of ‘behavior toward each other’ (Schachter 1899) is a real sectarian-forming force. His charismatic personality contained such features as the ability to reach a professional equilibrium coupled with strict moral rules.
