More about Projection: Before and Beyond

Marika Henriques

Marika Henriques

54 Campbell Court, Gloucester Road, London SW7 4PD

Marika Henriques  

The ‘thought’ which Jan McGregor Hepburn's interesting article Before and Beyond Projection? (British Journal of Psychotherapy, 9(1)), posed on problems surrounding the issue of ‘holding patients in mind’, activated my own ‘thinking’. I began to speculate about what the frustration might be, which when not tolerated might result, instead of thinking, in the ‘bad object’ and projective identification. I began to wonder about the idea which might lie behind the notion of being a ‘bad therapist’, were one to attend to patients in the particular ‘holding in mind’ described in the article, rather than maintaining a ‘proper therapeutic attitude’ which normally offers effective interpretation.

Besides Winnicott's ideas on ‘primary maternal preoccupation’, the concept which helped me most to clarify issues, was what in Jungian psychology is called ‘participation mystique’. Jung borrowed the term from the anthropologist Levy-Bruhl and then developed it further. He defined it (1921) as a ‘particular kind of psychological connection … which consists in the fact that the subject cannot clearly distinguish himself from the object, but is bound to it by direct relationship which amounts to partial identity’. This sounds much like projection of the usual kind. But Marie-Louise von Franz (1959) pointed out that ‘we can only speak of projection in the proper sense of the word … when the feeling identity is disturbed’. Projection implies ‘that the person is already to a certain extent out of the participation mystique, or archaic identity, until then there is no projection’. This seems to indicate that participation exists prior to the dawn of consciousness, that it is a process ‘before and beyond projection’. Indeed Jung talked of participation also as a ‘mutual unconsciousness’. He said that 'because the basic structure of the mind is the same in everybody, we cannot make distinctions when we experience on that level. There we do not know if something has happened to you or to me. And if what the patient projects into the analyst is identical with the analyst's own unconscious content, then there is a dangerous process going on, where analyst and patient mutually project into each other. Then they both fall into the same ‘dark hole of unconsciousness’ and get into the condition of participation. He wrote (1946): ‘This situation is difficult and distressing for both parties; often the doctor is in much the same position as the alchemist who no longer knew whether he was melting the mysterious amalgam in the crucible or whether he was the salamander glowing in the fire’.

Individual Psychotherapy Trainings: A Guide by Jan Abram. Published by Free Association Books, London, 1992; 307 pages; £17.95.

Anna Witham

Anna Witham

London

Anna Witham  

Psychotherapy is coming of age in Britain - this excellent and useful book and the new UK Council for Psychotherapy are witness to this. This is a book to be welcomed by a wide variety of people -potential psychotherapists and their teachers, training therapists and supervisors and, because it is also addressed to ‘the general public who may be needing help’, to potential patients. As the author's overall intention is to ‘demystify psychotherapy’, the question for her reviewer is how far she has succeeded in accomplishing this task for the lay person as well as the interested and potential professional.

From the many therapy organisations that are now in existence, Abrams has chosen to concentrate on individual one-to-one psychotherapy for adults, and in her book she has focused on the two largest and most common types of therapeutic help available, the psychoanalytical psychotherapies and the humanistic psychotherapies. The book is a detailed catalogue of twenty-six of the individual adult psychotherapy organisations and trainings in Britain.

But before she embarks on the detailed examination of these organisations and the trainings they offer, she presents her readers with a review of psychotherapy, what it is and what it can offer. Here she outlines the different types and levels of psychotherapy that are available; she looks at the limitations of the availability of psychotherapy in the NHS; the emergence (not before time) of the then UKSCP. She then considers the two types of training, the analytic and the humanistic, what they really mean and something of the differences between them. She has structured her consideration of analytical psychotherapy, which she addresses in greater detail than the humanistic approach, by looking at four major areas of internal controversy; Freud and Jung; the issue of ‘lay analysis’; the differences and similarities between psychoanalysts and psychotherapists, and finally the question of psychoanalysis and homosexuality. In the section on humanistic psychotherapy no areas of controversy as such are discussed and she does not say why. One feels that the issue of the use of body work and massage in relation to the ‘talking cure’ might have been considered a controversial issue and that she herself might have something to say on this as she has moved from the humanistic background of her earlier training to working more psychoanalytically. However, this aside, readers whether initiated or uninitiated into the complexities of psychotherapy, will find a great deal of valuable information in this chapter.

London

Charles Rycroft  

In his Introduction, which is in fact a full-length contribution, Laurence Spurling discusses tradition in general terms and draws attention to the numerous ambiguities inherent in it, notably the fact that tradition is both the integrating, stabilising factor that holds societies, and indeed individuals, together and also that which must be rebelled against and questioned if anyone within society is to be original and creative. He also points out the dialectical relationship between tradition and treason; once an ideology or a way of life becomes a tradition, it can be treason to oppose or reject it. He then goes on to discuss the fact that psychoanalysis began as a revolutionary, subversive movement devoted to the liberation of the individual from the authority of his parents, but that nowadays 'much analytically inspired writing comes over as deeply traditional, with an overwhelming priority placed on a knowledge of and respect for what has gone before, somewhat reminiscent of the style of Talmudic scholarship.

The seven contributors (including Spurling) all have in common various things that they are not. Not one calls him (or her)self a psychoanalyst or an analytical psychologist, nor takes any cognisance of what many people would regard as the dominant psychoanalytical tradition, the one which was transmitted from Vienna by Anna Freud and Heinz Hartmann and which is now represented by the Contemporary Freudians in this country and by the ego-psychologists in America. (The number of analysts who are not listed in the Name Index is impressive: Kohut, Kernberg, Hartmann, Bowlby, Meltzer; Fairbairn only scrapes in with one reference, and Anna Freud is mentioned only as her father's patient and as Klein's opponent.)

Haya Oakley

London

Haya Oakley  

But what we have here is only the effect of the analyst's passions: his fear, which is not error, but ignorance, his taste, which is not to satisfy, but not to disappoint either, his need, which is not to govern, but to keep the upper hand. It has nothing to do with any counter-transference on the part of this or that individual; it is a question of the consequences of the dual relation, if the therapist does not overcome it, and how can he overcome it if he sees it as the ideal of his action? (J Lacan)

This passage from Lacan's paper on the direction of the cure and the principles of its power accompanied my reading of this book as it captures so aptly my sole substantial reservation, namely that it is not the ideas proposed but the basic philosophy behind them that is called into question.

This is a clear, yet passionately written book emanating, by the author's own admission, from his search for answers to some fundamental questions at the heart of the psychoanalytic enterprise: the nature of perception, the nature of the self, the capacity to separate and the possibility of symbol formation, to name but a few. Dr Wright avoids unnecessary use of jargon and displays an enviable talent at expressing very complex ideas in a clear, ordinary, at times poetic and always personal style.

Far from displaying any personal ignorance, Dr Wright makes use of his wide knowledge of philosophy, poetry, literature and psychology in his attempt to address these issues. But he is ultimately unable to overcome his basic concept of the ‘dual relation’ being all there is at the beginning of life and not making the leap I was hoping for to a truly phenomenological critique.

The promise and the problematic of this book are illustrated in the language of one of its opening phrases when Dr Wright states that, ‘something that phenomenologically is outer may really be something inner that has been projected’ (p. xiv). He goes on to say that he could have been explaining the ‘look’ of the other as ‘having been invaded by a primitive oral-incorporative aspect of the subject’. He does not reject such a reading but claims that it could not be accompanied in this project. Such a statement runs the risk of mixing fundamentalism with Darwinism as it is precisely such notions of interiority and exteriority in relation to the subject and the world which are at the very heart of the phenomenological critique of such psychoanalytic presuppositions.

Dear Jim and Michael

It's a good idea to publish your dialogues and letters to each other as a way of making an amusing and informal book about what psychotherapy has not achieved and how much more politically influential it could usefully be. You aim for spontaneity and, although there are some ponderous flippancies which show this reader anyway that Americans and English do not necessarily laugh at the same things, the method does make a book which can be read by practitioners and public. I would have it as a book to be dipped into because you avoid being ‘linear’ and sequential, and there is much knowledge, wordly awareness and ideas about mythology and cultural trends in the various letters and bits of dialogue.

There is a main basis for the discussion, the focus you might say, reminding us that focus is the Latin for hearth, where Hestia is the goddess, paired with Hermes the communicator, the messenger. My association, in the sort of apparent non-sequitur way characteristic of your book, was to Jung's autobiographical description in Memories, Dreams, Reflections of the building of The tower which represented his self - at the centre he built ‘the maternal hearth’. Jung the communicator was experiencing the maternal hearth as his centre, giving him a focus. In fact, this bit of linking is not really unconnected and is rather what you are, I believe, doing - pointing out to your readers that in the world of psychotherapy - or rather, therapy, as you say most of the time - we conceptualise linking in too narrow a framework, missing the age-long archetypcal experiences which inform the unconscious and thus our behaviour.

So, your main focus is that if therapists stick too rigidly to ‘the dogma of interiorisation’ they contribute to social fragmentation: individualisation has gone too far, it is necessary to understand collective needs and to relate individual to social group. This is a theme and a process which we, in Europe, are now plunged into again. Our own goddess, Margaret of Monetarism, said something to the effect that there is no society, only individuals. Her fellow Olympians, minor and Major, have used the appeal of the need to individuate (feel individual) to break down our collective organisations, nationally planned to foster communication and individual development. Are we now trending in the same direction as you, Jim and Michael, say of the United States, of proposing remedies for breakdowns which actually have social dysfunction as their cause?

UKCP and the National Register for Psychotherapy

Emmy van Deurzen-Smith

Emmy van Deurzen-Smith

London NW1 4NS

Emmy van Deurzen-Smith  

In January 1993 the United Kingdom Council for Psychotherapy was established as the national umbrella body for psychotherapy. It emerged after many hard years of work, initially through the Rugby Conferences, then since 1989 through the United Kingdom Standing Conference for Psychotherapy. One of the aims of having a national organisation was to be able to provide the public with a Register of Psychotherapists. This Register was launched in May at the Houses of Parliament in the presence of representatives of the Department of Health and the Under-Secretary of State, Timothy Yeo. Many other significant political figures attended, including the opposition spokesperson for health, David Blunkett MP, Graham Bright MP who introduced the 1981 Psychotherapy Bill to Parliament, and Lord Clinton-Davies who has supported us from the outset.

Consistent efforts on the part of the delegates of UKCP's 70 organisations have finally come to fruition. Complex issues of inclusion and exclusion have had to be tackled in the process. Agreements have had to be reached about appropriate standards for the many psychotherapeutic approaches represented.

UKCP now has a set of general entry and training criteria for organisations, an ethical code, a code of practice and a complaints procedure. In addition all organisations must abide by the criteria of their Section. These separate Section criteria allow for adjustment to the individual differences between various psychotherapeutic approaches, although all must adhere to the minimum standards agreed across the Council as a whole.

The first Register will hold the names of the practitioner members of current organisations, put forward by those organisations meeting the agreed standards. After this initial process of grandparenting only approved training and accrediting organisations will be able to add names to the Register. Because of this there has been some concern that not all qualified psychotherapists will have access to the Register. A process of accreditation for psychotherapists in this situation, for instance those with foreign qualifications, will be put into place through each of the Sections. This is of tremendous importance if the Register is to do justice to all those who are bona fide trained practitioners and who therefore have a right to appear on a National Register. Now that the public will begin to discriminate as to whether therapists are on the Register, and indeed will be able to find therapists simply by referring to the Register, we must ensure that no trained therapist who works to sound standards is disenfranchised. This will be of great importance also in our next phase of development as we move the profession on to statutory registration.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood  

There is a continuing question over psychotherapy's social and cultural place. The idea of the typical ‘yavi’ patient (young, attractive, verbal, intelligent) has worn thinner over the years; as well as the image of white, self-indulgent, middle-class, WoodyAllen-followers cracking at the seams. Particularly with the development of NHS psychotherapy - outside London as well as within the M25 web -class constraints have been eroded. However, the cultural divide remains fairly impervious. The proportions of black patients in psychotherapy does not seem to be commensurate with the size of that population; and certainly the number of black psychotherapy is tiny compared with the indigenes.

In this issue a number of aspects of race have been considered; and social bars are examined from various points of view. Barbara Fletchman Smith has noted the link with abuse. Carribean culture was founded in the abuse of the slave trade, and she argues that it has retained a central place, a ‘cultural introject’ as it were. It hovers as a focus both in the treatments of individuals and in the cultural influences which determine referral of people from that culture. Using an empirical method, Paul Gordon tests the openness of the profession to would-be trainees - we keep them white, he finds. He requires that in common with other professions we should adopt a formal policy of equal opportunities, and a monitoring system.

Being psychotherapists we have a ‘binocular vision’; in addition to social causes and constraints we like, maybe prefer, to examine internal factors. It is anyway our special area of expertise. Richard Tan has gone back to clinical work to look at those factors at work in the psychotherapeutic setting. He argues that when therapist and patient are from different cultures primitive mechanisms sustain an unspoken racial context which, uninterpreted, can lead to impasse. He stops short of saying that racism simply comes out of internal factors. However it is common enough for psychotherapists to ‘psycho-analyse’ racism and racist attitudes. There is no doubt that human psychology can dispose to forming the antagonisms, debasement and abuse that constitute racism. However what predisposes the human psyche, in bulk, to conform to parallel antipathies in separate cultural groups? Paul Gordon in his second piece reflects on the merits of psycho-analytic versus sociological points of view. He concludes that racism is almost a metaphor for the problem an individual has in sustaining his own boundary free from the interference of others. Such a non-interference theory links individual psychology with the social phenomenon of racism.

Uncontained in Mind and Body: Eating Disorders in Final Year Students

Nicola Hirsch

Nicola Hirsch

104/108 Bolsover Street, London W1P 7HF

Nicola Hirsch  

The paper describes a number of final year students with eating disorders. The students shared a ‘feeling’ that they were unable to live independently. Having difficulty containing and experiencing their psychological life, they were also unable to feel physically contained. The notion of the skin as a container is developed and extended to the lining of the digestive system and the paper explores disturbances in the students' perception of this system. Lacking a sense of a permeable ‘digestive boundary’ between internal and external, they equally lack a sense of self and other as seen in their relationship to the Polytechnic. Defending themselves against experiences of separation their wish is to be inside a refuge and their presenting anxiety is the fear that the impending end of their course will threaten them with expulsion and disintegration. In their symbiotic relationship to the Polytechnic the students are understood to be replicating an early relationship to their mother that predates a differentiation between psyche and soma.

Klaus Fink

Klaus Fink

Klaus Fink  

Firstly I must state that this patient, her scant history and her treatment plus the detailed two sessions left a sad impression on me. I already sensed the impotence, disturbance and aggression felt by both, patient and therapist, when I read the introduction and history, even before reading the details of the two sessions.

The first problem I encountered was that I could not find any working hypothesis regarding diagnosis, personality structure, defences, aetiology and treatment plan. There was a good description of the patient in general and of the interaction between patient and therapist but no plan or formulation about the understanding of the case. I myself feel uneasy if at some stage in my work with a patient I have not established some working hypothesis about a possible aetiology, the involved dynamics, the external and internal factors and a foreseeable prognosis.

After reading the therapist's account, Miss X seemed to me very ill, adopting a passive-aggressive stance that made her almost unreachable. Her ability to provoke a negative and angry counter-transference reaction in the therapist made her in my eyes a sadistic person but, of course, with the complementary masochistic elements. After reading the details of both sessions I was left with the impression of having witnessed a tug of war with no winner.

[[RunningHead]]

Commentary by a Tavistock-Trained Child Psychotherapist

Margaret Rustin

Margaret Rustin

Margaret Rustin  

These sessions record a mutually painful interaction. Miss X conveys an experience of being with an object that she believes wants something from her which she does not have to give. Her therapist feels that she/he is being rejected and prevented from offering the understanding which could bring relief. Yet the patient is attached to this frustrating interchange - so we can surmise that something crucial is being lodged in the relationship with her therapist, and that she has not given up hope that communication can be achieved. Her presence refutes her claim to being contented with her solitary confinement but it may be an enactment of her belief that she is imprisoned by an unavailable object.

What ideas might her history put in our minds? She offers no information about the living members of her family nor does she speak of current relationships with friends, fellow-students, teachers etc. … There is no discernible interest in the life around her. The most lively person in her mind seems to be her dead father. His personality is presented as dominated by violence. She recalls being attacked by him and we hear of his suicide. The violence was uncontrollable and of murderous quality. He found no one to contain it and she gives no evidence of believing there was any protection available for her. This is echoed in the story of abuse by a teacher which went unreported as, I would suggest, she had no idea that anyone would hear her complaint. She seems to have resorted to placing herself at a great distance from her pain, and to have believed that this was the way in which psychic survival could be achieved. She cannot, then, afford to come closer to her emotionality, yet seems to have become aware that this sort of survival is equivalent to living suicide. Emerging from her detachment would entail a fear of encountering a violent, abusive, exciting and unreliable object.

The unnamed mother and sister suggest an early infantile experience of feeling unrecognised, named, or claimed by her mother. The possibility of severe maternal depression during Miss X's early childhood might speculatively be linked with her mother's hidden history: does the East European background conceal enforced flight from a persecuting homeland either during the years of Soviet occupation of the Eastern bloc or from the Nazi threat in a previous generation?

Melanie Klein: From Theory to Reality by Otto Weininger. Published by Karnac Books, London, 1992; 210 pages; £16.95.

Giovanna Ceglie

Giovanna Ceglie

London

Giovanna Ceglie  

After a panoramic foreward by James Grotstein on the history, development, migration and receptivity of Kleinian ideas, followed by a brief biography of Klein by the author, we learn in the introduction the aims of the book. They are two: one, to outline the basic aspects of Melanie Klein's theories and the other, to suggest, in the words of the author, their range of application by drawing upon his vast experience as child psychotherapist and psychologist. The book is written for students or practitioners in child psychology. It has five chapters, the first on the schizo-paranoid position, the second on the depressive position, the third on the Oedipal phase, the fourth is on a Kleinian approach to elective mutism in children, and the fifth is a schematic resumé of Kleinian theories of infant psychic development.

Otto Weininger's endeavour to metabolise Klein's ideas, making them accessible and suggest their range of applications, all in 200 pages, in itself deserves recognition. With the first three chapters the reader is given the most exhaustive and comprehensible account of the vicissitudes of unconscious phantasy. The ubiquitousness of its operation is shown by numerous vignettes and observations of children and parents which make very interesting and alive reading. However anyone not already familiar with psychoanalytic theory and practice will not have much of an idea of where it all came from and how Klein came to develop her ideas in the way she did. More reference to Klein's ‘practice’ would have relieved the author of the burden of having to ‘prove’ the theory, a burden which is often evident when, to make a theoretical point, he makes people ‘talk’ Kleinan jargon.

Commentary by a Group Analyst

Dick Blackwell

Dick Blackwell

Dick Blackwell  

The content of this group certainly seems bizarre. However, the group takes place within a context which if it does not actually merit the designation ‘bizarre’ certainly has considerable potential for bizarreness! For me as a group analyst, context is particularly important. What is in the foreground must always be seen against a

258

background in order for it to be intelligible. There are a number of ways of looking at this group and I need to take a little space to explain the conceptual framework through which I would approach it.

Central to group analytic theory is the concept of matrix. This is the network of communication and shared meaning which develops in a group and through which members articulate both their individuality and their commonality. The matrix has two levels. The foundation matrix is the body of language, assumptions and experience, which all the members store prior to the inception of the group. So in this case we have a group who share the language and experience of being nurses in a large hospital in the north of England. This foundation matrix provides the basis for the development of a particular dynamic matrix which is the product of the evolving communication between the members in the particular group. The dynamic matrix is usually subdivided into four levels: reality content, transference, projective processes and archetypes or social unconscious. It is tempting to hypothesise about this group quite readily at these four levels as follows. Firstly, there are expressions of feeling about the realities of patient care, social life and a painful visit to the dentist. Then there is a mixed transference in which the facilitator is both the benign parent to whom these concerns can be brought, and the potentially threatening dentist whose explorations may bring up painful feelings. There is projection of disgustingness, monstrosity, handicap, hostility, sexuality, ferocity, etc., into patients, students and dentist. And there are undercurrents of social types such as hedonistic and irresponsible youth, asexual nurses, and damaged patients. But these speculations do not account for this particular group session. Nor do they necessarily suggest a way of working with this group. I would therefore seek to locate these hypotheses within a framework which would form the basis of my understanding and work with such a group. This framework would have four dimensions: social context (a loose but more self explanatory substitute for the term foundation matrix), structure, process, and content (these three being an alternative subdivision of the dynamic matrix.)

Joanna Ryan  

Both these original books take as their starting points the paucity of psychotherapeutic work with mentally handicapped people; they convincingly challenge the view that learning disabilities render psychoanalytic approaches inapplicable. Both show, with many illustrations, how people with various forms of handicap and disability can benefit from therapy that offers thought and reflection, how meaning can be found and restored in ‘stupid’ manifestations. Their demonstration of psychotherapeutic commitment and imagination is impressive and inspiring. It is also extraordinarily painful in what it reveals about the experience of handicap and disability, the defences elaborated to deal with unbearable realisations, and the many assaults, blows, traumas and failures dealt by inadequate or hostile environments. This is compounded by the constant reminder of the many factors that prevent or limit access by mentally handicapped people to psychotherapy. The financial and institutional resources needed to ensure that a severely handicapped person can attend sessions over a significant period of time are considerable, even where the value of such work is recognised and not felt as useless or threatening.

Valerie Sinason's book will undoubtedly be a landmark in this area for many years to come. Much can be learned from the range, depth and clarity of her case studies which vividly describe many different patients, most with handicaps of long-standing duration but including one patient with Alzheimer's disease. The detail with which she presents the progress (or otherwise) of the therapeutic work, including many of her comments and interpretations, is compelling and illuminating. We are enabled to see, for example, how the noises and actions of someone with no verbal speech at all can be responded to and interpreted, in ways that allow communication and meaning to be established and extended, with the consequent improvements in self-regard. We are shown how the commonly met phenomenon of self-destructive and self-mutilating behaviour can be tolerated within the consulting room, taken into the orbit of the relationship between the therapist and patient, made sense of, and ameliorated.

[[RunningHead]]

Love of Beginnings by J B Pontalis. Published by Free Association Books, London; 1993; 171 pages; £13.95.

Carlotta Johnson

Carlotta Johnson

Northumberland

Carlotta Johnson  

I chose to read this book for two reasons; first because I thought the title was so poetic, gave me pleasure, was like an invitation ‘to come and see, come and taste’ and second because for years I have had and used the thick scholarly tome, The Language of Psychoanalysis. The idea that this same author is writing something called Love of Beginnings - a lyrical meditation on his own life' to quote from the advertisement, well, that aroused my curiosity.

In the book Pontalis says many remarkable things. He writes a piece of literature and stresses the requirement he has for himself to live in several spaces, not just in a psychoanalytic one. He wrote while on vacation (vacances, a word that for him always rhymes with enfance) on the island, Belle-Ile. We can see the room where he sits, a room with a small window, open to the sky and the ocean. He goes there ‘in order to feel impelled to write in a more wandering way, a way that (in the end) has no other object than itself, a way that has come to be called literature’. The title in French is L'Amour des Commencements. This title illustrates an important paradix concerning beginnings; that they arise in conjunction with endings. In my adolescence the moment of leaving high school was sometimes called ‘The commencement’. this moment was marked by a public gathering with music, speeches and the giving of diplomas. I am interested by Commencement and the way this one word embodies completion of one thing and the beginning of another. I am sorry that I am not fluent in French, as many idioms and subtleties in Pontalis's language will be lost in the process of translation, the fact that still so many come through makes me envious of those readers who have more.

His style of writing draws the reader into the places and situations of the story. I am standing behind him and see the photograph of the boy with his father, the father's hand touching, resting on the boy's shoulder. Three days afterwards the father is dead and the boy becomes silent. It is so present. As I read along I come close to the sights, smells, feel of his School H, the Lycee, summers at Cabourg, the death of his grandmother, his friendships, lovers, his times of teaching, of studying. Pontalis returns again and again to the problem of language; how it tries to give shape to the shapeless, how when it loses its modesty and tries to impose too strongly on thought and experience how when it becomes a one-and-only, then in its tyranny it is abusive. He cannot accept such a use and in the story, as he moves from age to age, we see how he struggles, is silent, is mute, afraid of getting inside language because maybe he will never be able to move out of it.

[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood  

Training is a crucial issue which, at the same time, and perhaps for that reason, is the most contentious within British psychotherapy. Concerns about standards of training and practice have surfaced so strongly they have split the Standing Conference. A preliminary notice of the formation of the British Confederation of Psycho-Analytic Psychotherapy was published in the last issue. The Standing Conference itself also remains confident as the outgoing Chairman's address, in this issue, relates. * The split, bitter though it has been, needs calm appraisal.

Nearly two years ago, the Guild of Psychotherapists held a Study Day on fundamental issues of training psychotherapy. We are pleased to publish three of the papers presented there. Jonathon Pedder's paper addressed various points of ongoing discussion most prominently the fields from which candidates for psychotherapy training come. The debate centres on whether psychotherapists should have trained previously in one of the mental health professions - the so-called ‘core professions’. Naturally many doctors and psychologists think so. The temperature of the debate has been stoked up by the approach of Brussels and looming European conformity. These are momentous issues which readers will need to debate. Both Andrew Samuels and Karl Figlio contribute to the calmer reflection that needs to be the basis from which political heat should be generated. Both are exercised by the diversity of psychotherapy approaches and of psychotherapists themselves. Figlio is concerned about our need to externalise an objective assessment of good/bad practice and training and how misguided that endeavour is. The problem is to assess from the inside, and he attempts to scan many of the issues arising from that posture. Samuels' plea is for an even-handedness to difference, and to the frictions inevitably attendant on differences. Elitism can supervene instead of difference, with very distorting judgements on the needs of patients and of trainees.

T.T.S. Hayley (1913-1993)

Tom Hayley, Editor of the International Journal and Review of Psychoanalysis since 1978, died in June after a varied, rich and fulfilling life. His career spanned the fields of anthropology, the Indian Civil Service and the Institute of Psychoanalysis, where he worked diligently for over 40 years, serving to revise the organisation's rules of procedure, as a training analyst and as a Vice-President of the Society.

Tom's zest for living was punctuated by the unusual: piloting the early bi-planes; in Africa, being besieged overnight in a land rover by a lion, whose eyes glowing in the darkness did not prevent him from sleeping soundly; and, during his anthropological studies, observing the ritual removal of a ‘bad object’ from an unwell tribesman by a Lango medicine-man who then spat it into a gourd.

Tom took great pleasure from his farm in Kent, doing much of the work himself on the weekends, and enjoying his children and grandchildren. He was a friend, supervisor and analyst to many, and he shall be missed.

[[RunningHead]]

Technophobia and Technophilia

Barry Richards

Barry Richards

Essex RM8 2AS

Barry Richards  

‘Technology’ is a wide and often problematic term; I shall be using it here to refer to consumer goods which are the products of modern industry (and so will be straying into ‘consumption’ across the categories into which today's papers are placed). I will be drawing on psychoanalysis - amongst other intellectual resources - in an exploration of our attitudes towards these products, and in particular towards one very important consumer good, though some of the observations I want to make should also help to understand attitudes towards other goods, and indeed towards other forms of technology such as information and medical technologies.

I will use the terms technophilia and technophobia not to invent new diagnostic formulations, but as a way of highlighting how technologies evoke in us strong positive and negative feelings which impede rational discussion of them, and which produce reverential or dismissive attitudes rather than realistic appraisal of their social and environmental costs and benefits.

But, as a short preamble, let me first make an observation on the nature of this conference. When Ivan Ward, who has organised it, first told me about it, I thought what an excellent idea it was and wondered why no-one had organised it before. But I have a concern about what people here may be expecting from it. I suspect that a number of you will be hoping to hear an announcement of the marriage of psychoanalytic insight with environmentalist politics.

As quite a close and long-standing friend of both parties, I would take great pleasure in their betrothal. But in what I have to say, I will be pointing out that this relationship cannot be a completely harmonious one, and the blame for this would in a sense lie with psychoanalysis. Analysis is a relentlessly critical character. As we know, it refuses to take what people say at face value, and is constantly probing for a reality which is more complex and usually less congenial than is at first apparent. Because of its unyielding nature, psychoanalysis has had some failed relationships in the past with suitors from the world of politics. Some of us at one time held out great hopes for its relationship with Marxism. But, although they had some good times together, that liaison ran aground against the refusal of psychoanalysis to exempt anything from its analytic gaze, not least the murky unconscious of the revolutionary.

[[RunningHead]]

Prejudice and Homosexuality

Francesca Denman

Francesca Denman

1 Ham Common, Richmond, Surrey TW10 7JF

Francesca Denman  

The recent psychodynamic literature on homosexuality is reviewed and a negative view is shown to remain prevalent. It is suggested that this may be the result of prejudice as opposed to simple error or to justified belief. In order to support this suggestion a theory of the origins and operation of prejudice is outlined. Next it is shown to be a consequence of this theory that prejudice should be especially likely in the domain of sexuality. Then an understanding of the psychic mechanisms which maintain prejudice is applied to a close reading of three papers concerned with homosexuality, which are shown to retain the marks of prejudice despite their compassionate and thoughtful stance. The way in which the logical distortions which mark prejudice are discernible in all three papers and operate to perpetuate some prejudices about AIDS, HIV infection, homosexuality and perversion is also shown. The prevalence of prejudices about homosexuality is noted to be especially great amongst psychodynamic therapists. It is argued that some reasons for this lie in the nature of psychoanalytic theory particularly in the way that homosexuality challenges some choices implicit within psychoanalytic theory. The parallels between this situation and that of the prejudiced individual are noted and suggestions are made for steps that might reduce prejudice in this area. Finally it is argued that the ill effects of prejudice on theory in this area are detrimental to psychoanalysis as well as to homosexuals. Prejudice and its effects are argued to be major barriers to the construction of good theory about homosexuality and, more optimistically, the work of some analysts who have questioned the prevailing attitude to homosexuality is reviewed.

[[RunningHead]]

Self Psychology: Origins and Overview

Frank Lachmann

Frank Lachmann

393 West End Avenue 1-A, New York, NY 10024

Frank Lachmann  

The origins of Kohut's theory of self psychology can be found in Freud's metapsychology. In his first book The Analysis of the Self, Kohut, however, reversed the classical assumption that posits narcissism and object love to be in a see-saw relationship. He proposed separate lines of development for each, that is, an independent line of development for narcissism. Kohut's shift from a psychoanalytic focus on the narcissistic sector of the personality to a psychology of the self is outlined. The concept of ‘narcissistic transferences’ gave way to ‘selfobject transference’. The self psychological view of sexuality, aggression, resistance, psychosexual development, the Oedipal phase, transference and countertransference are presented. Treatment implications derived from these contributions are the most extensive and revolutionary aspect of Kohut's proposals. A case vignette illustrates Kohut's distinction between Oedipal conflict pathology and Oedipal phase manifestations.

Metaphysics as a Guide to Morals by Iris Murdoch. Published by Chatto & Windus, London, 1992; 520 pages; £20.

John Heaton

John Heaton

London

John Heaton  

‘Metaphysics’ and ‘morals’ are not exactly buzz words in psychotherapy. Freud in 1901, on the crest of the popular belief that science can provide the answer to pretty well everything, proudly declared that the psychology of the unconscious will explain ‘the myths of paradise and the fall of man, of God, of good and evil, of immortality, and so on, and to transform metaphysics into metapsychology’ (The Psychopathology of Everyday Life). Few scientists took much notice of this declaration. If we look, for example, at the founders of the two most important scientific theories in this century, relativity and quantum mechanics, we find that they were deeply influenced by metaphysical thought; Einstein by Hume and Kant, Niels Bohr by Kierkegaard, Schrodinger by Schopenhauer and Vedanta, Heisenberg by Plato. As the century draws to its close there is little evidence that metaphysical thinking is finished, let alone being replaced by metapsychology; as so often before in its long history, it has changed direction according to the times.

One way for psychotherapists to approach this book is through the thought of Bion. In his later work Bion wrote about ‘0’ which was the sign he used to denote ‘ultimate reality’, that which does not fall into the domain of knowledge; he claimed it could ‘become’ but cannot be ‘known’ and that during therapy the analyst must focus his or her attention on it. Bion is a bit crude compared to traditional metaphysicians; for example, if ‘0’ cannot be known how does Bion know it can ‘become’? And how can one focus one's attention on ‘something’ that is not known? Thus how does one know it is a something rather than a nothing? Nevertheless he made a start. Roughly speaking, metaphysics is the study of ‘0’.

The study of ‘0’ must be strictly differentiated from the study of the unconscious which is the domain of psychoanalysis. The unconscious connotes those contents of the mind that are not present in the field of consciousness; these contents include ‘representations’ of the instincts, childhood wishes that have become fixated and so on. Its activity obeys certain rules such as condensation and displacement. All of this is known by psychoanalysts who claim scientific status: ‘science’ of course means systematic knowledge of something.

Francesca Bion introduces Cogitation with the remark that this series of entries from Bion's notebooks is ‘the last of the posthumous publications, which have given me so much pleasure to prepare’. It is a fascinating addition to the canon.

We can see clearly how Bion was drawn to many of the possibilities in Klein's 1935 paper on the depressive position, and was able to rework the concepts of paranoid schizoid and depressive positions to a point at which they owed only a nominal relationship to Klein's theory. Many of the entries reveal how he came to believe that thinking entailed some persistent oscillation between the paranoid schizoid and the depressive positions, in place of some notion of an enduring linear development:

In the chaos of unconnected, incoherent facts I see the point -the selected fact. If I am wise, I reject it and reassume chaos … And may not this give rise to situations in which the patient appears enviously to reject an interpretation that he accepted the day before? Barbara Lloyd

Barbara Lloyd

Sussex

Barbara Lloyd  

This, the sixteenth volume in The New Library of Psychoanalysis series, presents a theory of the origins of mental life still relatively unknown to those who read psychoanalytic theory only in English. The distinguished British psychoanalyst, Adam Limentani, has drawn together thirteen papers by Eugenio Gaddini (1916-1985) and organised them around three intertwined themes: imitation, formation of the ego and its separate objects, and the meaningfulness of the body to the mind. Although seven of these papers have already had disparate publication in English, monolingual readers are here provided with a coherent exposition of the work of this pioneering Italian psychoanalyst.

Eugenio Gaddini's particular focus was the development of psychic life in infancy, an interest shared with the creators of English Object Relations theory, Melanie Klein and Donald Winnicott. Psychotherapists already steeped in this tradition will find Gaddini's work, which he also linked with that of Phyllis Greenacre, truly international, encompassing concerns in both European and American psychoanalysis.

Trained in classical instinct theory with its emphasis on the centrality of the Oedipus complex, Gaddini sought to expand psychoanalytic understanding of mental life in the first three years of life through use of his own clinical knowledge and modern observational studies. Imitation has a particular importance as Gaddini proposed that by the middle of the first year an enfant has acquired a mental sense of its body drawn from the sensations which arise through experience, registered by the body but not a simple reflection of actual biological experience. Although the physiological body can exist without mental functioning, it is in the early registration of bodily experience that the mind-body continuum comes into existence. The pre-symbolic nature of this development, through which bodily experience is translated into mental sense, brings the reader up against formidable difficulties in grasping the momentous, yet elusive nature of the changes the theory seeks to describe.

Bob Hinshelwood  

Frank Lachman introduces us to self-psychology - those of us in Britain who have been slow to pick up on what has been developing in the United States. It is a ‘new’ theory of narcissism, a personality characteristic which, in psycho-analysis, has often had a bad press. The nurturing of the self - and even by the self - was given a radical change of priority by Kohut. Lachman in an admirably clear presentation has outlined Kohut's challenge to the view that the more narcissistic the self the less object-related it can be. Instead, it is actually from a secure narcissism or security of the sense of self (what is sometimes called positive narcissism) that the ability to form object-relations stems. In a very contrasting vein, one that represents the source of a much more recognisably British view of narcissism, Kenneth Sanders describes the same sense of well-being in terms of internal objects; and develops the point that a rich sense of self can become the fulcrum of a conflict. He employs the notion of a kind of ‘negative narcissism’ which continually threatens the internal sense of well-being.

Clearly British analysts and therapists have grown up in a different professional, social, ideological climate from American ones. Our views of the nature of human beings have taken radically divergent paths - in a sense, Epicurean versus Manichean. How this has come about would be a fascinating study in cultural history; but that it exists is the important fact we need to retain. As with our patients, when we listen to each other we need to know where ‘each is coming from’. Liam Clarke starts from an understanding of the full effects of the cultural setting to, as it were, put rational emotive therapy in its place - its place is the contemporary abrasive political climate of the rational, entrepreneurial individual. He goes on to put most other therapies in their place too. The knowledge of cultural setting can be a heavy weapon for dismissing schools of thought that claim an absolutist knowledge of people. Staying with the United States, Jeremy Holmes brings us news of divergences in California, the land of radical divergence. This has led to his reflections on the adversarial nature of British public life and its possible effects on the development of psycho-analysis and psychotherapy in Britain. Perhaps it is not therefore surprising that many of us in Britain feel we understand the ubiquitous importance of splitting, and work that concept pretty hard.

Christopher Fortune

Christopher Fortune

11 Hummingbird Lane, Bowen Island, BC, Canada VON 1GO

Christopher Fortune  

The recent publication of Sandor Ferenczi's Clinical Diary (1988), written in 1932, is a rich source of material on Ferenczi and his last ideas. The diary has given us access to Ferenczi's most intimate thoughts and feelings about his therapeutic work and his relationship with Freud. It has also revealed unknown aspects of Ferenczi's life and work: his experiment in mutual analysis, his discovery of his own early childhood traumas, and a detailed look at the therapeutic process which culminated in his final published papers, specifically his radical classic, ‘Confusion of Tongues Between Adults and the Child’ (1933). Along with historical perspectives on Ferenczi, the diary has also introduced a number of Ferenczi's last patients, most particularly ‘R.N.’, the critically important, yet virtually unknown woman whose analytic treatment dominated Ferenczi's final years.

‘R.N.’ was Ferenczi's code-name for Elizabeth Severn, an early American ‘psychotherapist’ whose chronic symptoms and desperate mental state led her to seek the help of the famous Hungarian analyst. Severn's case - as R.N. - fills the diary's pages and establishes her profound influence on Ferenczi, and her role in his final radical challenge to classical psychoanalysis and to Freud himself. His ‘principal patient’, Severn was in analysis with Ferenczi in Budapest for eight years - from 1924 until just before his death in 1933. Elizabeth Severn's case and her analytic relationship with Ferenczi is an important paradigm case, a pivotal point in the history and development of psychoanalysis in the tradition of Anna 0 and Dora. Through her initiation of the experiment in mutual analysis, Severn was the catalyst for Ferenczi's recognition of the clinical significance of countertransference (Wolstein 1989). She was also a critical factor in his early understanding of the dynamics of childhood sexual trauma, including his own. This understanding led Ferenczi to reconsider Freud's early trauma theory; in doing so, he challenged Freud and questioned psychoanalysis' emphasis on unconscious fantasy. In fact, Elizabeth Severn may have been the first sexually abused analysand whose actual childhood trauma was the focus of psychoanalytic treatment since Freud abandoned his so-called ‘seduction theory’ in the late 1890's (Fortune 1989, 1993).

Who Owns Psychoanalysis?

Jeremy Holmes

Jeremy Holmes

Raleigh Park, Barnstaple, Devon EX31 4JB

Jeremy Holmes  

Two nations separated by everything except their language - this was Churchill's verdict on the US-UK (and probably his parental) relationship. But when it comes to the word ‘psychoanalyst’ the linguistic divide is as great as the cultural and geographical. In the field of psychotherapy, where the British like adjectives, Americans prefer nouns: we have psychoanalytic psychotherapists, they have psychoanalysts. In the US, as in Britain, the title psychoanalyst is not protected by law. There is nothing to stop anyone calling themselves a psychoanalyst - indeed it is common to see advertisements in the Californian alternative press of the type: ‘Colonic Irrigation, and Psychoanalysis - first session free!’

It is easy to sneer at such linguistic abuse - seeing it perhaps in Chasseguet-Smirgelian (1985) terms as the faecal world of the oedipally envious. In Britain we tend to smile in a smug way at such absurdities knowing that it could never happen here -rather as we do about tribal violence and religious bigotry, while turning a blind eye to what is happening in Northern Ireland. But with the advent of registration of psychotherapists, titles have suddenly become very important in Britain - as those caught up in the struggle between the Analytic section of the UKSCP and the Confederation of British Psychotherapists well know. A lecture trip to California allowed for a closer consideration of the American psychoanalytic scene and its implications for the UK.

Recently a group of senior Californian psychoanalysts decided to break away from the Californian branch of the American Psychoanalytic Association (APA) and to set up the Institute for Contemporary Psychoanalysis (ICP) (Breger 1992). Their directors include Louis Breger, Robert Stolorow and British-born and trained Victoria Hamilton; corresponding members include Christopher Bolas, Charles Rycroft and - to declare an interest - the author. The ICP is a ‘free-standing’ training organisation which, while fully ‘psychoanalytic’ in its values, is not recognised by the APA. The reasons for the secession were numerous. Many of the leaders are psychologists still smarting from the prolonged rearguard action of the APA against the admission of non-medical members - a battle that was eventually ‘lost’ only after a psychologist pursued the issue through the courts. They were concerned about the implicit ruling of the APA which makes it impossible for homosexuals to be accepted for psychoanalytic training. They objected to the hierarchical and infantilising structure of the psychoanalytic training programmes in which students have little say in the content of their courses, and attempts to alter this tend to be interpreted as evidence of insufficient analysis rather than valid criticism.

My Friendship with Miksa Schachter

Sandor Ferenczi

Sandor Ferenczi

Budapest

Sandor Ferenczi  

I first met Miksa Schachter in 1898 under unusual circumstances. I was a junior physician at the Rokus Hospital. While I wanted to become a neurologist, Kalman Muller's malice chained me to the VD (‘prostitutes’) department for more than a year. I had requested many times to be liberated from duties that were so alien to me. All in vain - the hospital director, who was so strict with his subordinates, turned down all my requests. As I had no chance to perform psychological experiments, I had begun to experiment on myself. I had tried to explore the so-called ‘occult’ phenomena, amongst others. It happened once that, following a dinner with friends, I walked through the permanently locked gates of the ‘Little Rokus’1 well after midnight. I went to the junior physicians' room and engaged in ‘automatic writing’, frequently discussed by the spiritualists of the time; Janet had already published interesting observations on this phenomenon. It occurred to me that it was already very late; I was tired and somewhat aroused emotionally. All these circumstances favoured the exploration. So I picked up a pencil and, holding it loosely in my hand, I pressed it against a piece of blank paper. I decided to let the pencil move ‘on its own’, letting it write whatever it wished. Senseless scribbles came first, then letters, words (some of them strange to me), and finally whole sentences. Soon I was having a real dialogue with my pencil - I asked questions and got quite unexpected answers. Being young, first of all I demanded answers to big theoretical problems, but later more practical questions occurred to me. Finally the pencil suggested the following: ‘Write an article on spiritualism for Gyogyaszat, the editor will be interested’.

I had arrived from Vienna not long before and knew hardly anything about Hungarian medical journals. I did not know that, while Orvosi Hetilap (Medical Weekly)2 was the journal of the influential university circles, Gyogyaszat (Therapy)3 was the forum of a single powerful man - Miksa Schachter. His voluntarily undertaken crusade was to protect medical justice and ethics from threatening attacks by any antagonists.

Imagination and the Psychotherapeutic Process

William Barnes-Gutteridge

William Barnes-Gutteridge

Stirling FK9 4LA

William Barnes-Gutteridge  

Imagination is a neglected topic in psychoanalysis and in psychotherapy because we have an inadequate conception of the phenomenon. This inadequate conception renders imaginative activity intractable to investigation. I offer a framework for thinking about imagination that remedies this defect, and I show how we might use this framework to develop a procedure by which to investigate different kinds of imaginative activity. I illustrate this procedure by investigating the kinds of imaginative activity that support two mental abilities. One is our ability to respond to fictional objects (characters in novels). The other is our ability to respond to the mental states of others - an ability I refer to as psychological understanding. Phantasy characteristically operates to block an imaginative understanding of others. And I propose that a fundamental condition for a person to achieve normal object relationships is an ability to imagine the mental life of another person. I conclude by suggesting how this framework allows us to investigate a psychotherapeutic culture. And I outline an approach to investigate the psychotherapeutic culture of a residential therapeutic community.

Reading Perversion

Duncan Barford

Duncan Barford

Duncan Barford  

This paper argues that disavowal, the mechanism underlying perversion, is by its very nature self-contradictory and cannot be fully accounted for by either of Freud's psychical topographies. It is suggested that successive theorists have failed to solve this problem adequately, but have tended to discuss perversion in terms more appropriate to either neurosis or psychosis. This paper proposes that perversion displays a radically unique style of defence; it is described how this differs from repression in particular. Finally it is shown how analysis of the rhetoric of perverse fantasy can clarify the nature of this unique defensive strategy.

Commentary from an Independent Psycho-Analyst

Victor Sedlak

Victor Sedlak

Victor Sedlak  

I want to begin by noting how impressed I was by this work and the tremendous effort the therapist puts into trying to understand his patient. (I'm not sure why I quickly began to feel that the therapist is male; if this impression is wrong then I apologise. I'll refer to the therapist as he in this commentary.) I was also admiring of the therapist's honesty in describing very difficult counter-transference feelings. Much of what the therapist interprets is excellent but there is a central point that could have been focused on more in the sessions. It is a point that the therapist indicates in his overall description of the treatment: ‘… she often opens up just at the end of the session, mostly telling me something worrying about herself, thus leaving me in a state of concern for her wellbeing until I see her next’. It is interesting that there is then a new paragraph which begins: ‘Miss X seems to use her treatment predominantly to evacuate her feelings. Hence I often feel the container of unmanageable emotions of which she wants to rid herself’. The therapist goes on to describe these but I think he actually has the nub of the problem in that previous sentence. The point I wish to develop is that the patient has an unfaceable anxiety that her destructiveness is causing extreme emotional damage to her therapist. I will try to argue this point in terms of her history later but first I want to indicate how this appears to me in the clinical material.

The first session begins with the therapist's state of health as the paramount concern. The patient seems unable to investigate this very thoroughly beyond asking him if he is all right. There are then various long silences interspersed with broken, incomplete utterances and various attempts by the therapist to help the patient communicate. These interpretations gradually focus on there being something cruel and destructive, either in the therapist or in the patient, and also on an anxiety that the therapist is not strong enough to withstand this and he cites his illness as adding to this anxiety. This makes the patient defensive and appear to feel as though something might be used against her. The therapist interprets her anxiety and, in particular, her fear that he will use something against her. The patient smiles awkwardly but soon says she cannot think. The therapist interprets her attack on thinking and then adds the words that produce the turning point of the session: that the patient keeps BOTH of them at the level of not thinking. There is a dramatic response to this interpretation: the patient says she fears breaking down and losing her mind. From that point in the session there is only one anxious person in the room and that is the therapist who is very concerned about the state of his patient.

Jafar Kareem

Nina Coltart

Nina Coltart

Nina Coltart  

My good friend, Jafar Kareem, died suddenly and unexpectedly last year - and too soon: it is too bad there is no one to blame for deaths which we consider clumsily handled and badly mistimed. Jafar had the energy and ideas to pour into his life and work for another 20 years: why on earth snatch away him, of all people, when there are unhappy, ill old people longing for the Great Reaper to come and scythe them down? Of course the big mistake Jafar made was to choose to be born with certain genes which were going to dictate the particular shape he ended up with - a typically merry, endomorphic, pyknic individual; if he had been a bus, he would have had ‘Coronary’ written up on his front notice board. And that was what happened. His gallant frame succumbed - mercifully quickly - to a massive coronary thrombosis and, instead of a hateful life condemned to cardiac invalidism, Jafar was with us no more. And what an enormous gap he left, this short, stocky, joky man, a great crater which covers a huge are of North London - to say the very least. For all I know, there are equivalent craters in Pakistan, Israel, Austria - all places where the indefatigable Jafar made his mark, won friends and influenced people.

When I first heard his life story - he told it to me himself, sitting in my living room one day soon after we had met - I was simply spellbound. I felt like those two boys sitting on the ground in the Pre-Raphaelite picture, The Boyhood of Raleigh, in which the boys are rapt in the presence of a storyteller (Raleigh himself?). It was difficult to absorb Jafar's life story all at once, one could hardly credit that he had fitted so much in. He was born in Calcutta, and was the youngest of a large family. His earliest life was clearly happy and stable - he could never have achieved all he did without solidly internalised good figures.

[[RunningHead]]

Clinical Commentary XIV

[The infant observation as presented here was sent ‘blind’ to three people who represent different therapeutic schools of thought. They were asked to comment in such a way as to bring out the differences between ways of thinking about infants, about this particular infant and about the task of infant observation in general - Ed]

The Therapist Writes

Background to Observation

The observation family consists of Victor and Anna, an educated couple in their mid-30's both with careers in creative design, and Peter, aged 2'/Z, a lively and bright boy. Victor works shifts, enabling him to have some daytime at home. Anna works freelance and was expecting initially to return to work about five months after the birth. The family live in a Victorian terraced house furnished inexpensively but with thought and colour. The state of the interior reflects varying degrees of jumble and serious mess as if a statement of priorities is being made. Toys and baby equipment predominate with an emphasis on educational value and creative play.

Victor was actively sharing in the childcare and was the sole carer during three visits out of the first twelve, as well as being present for some of the earlier ones following Joanne's birth when he was occupied with managing the house and Peter. He had pushed for children while Anna had hoped to put this off for longer. She thought that he was the better mother of the two. Although Anna had had a long and difficult birth with Peter, her fears of a repetition were not realised with Joanne who also proved to be an easier baby all round. Baby Joanne had blonde hair and large blue eyes like her mother and was alert and responsive.

At the first meeting I was assailed by intense feelings of discomfort at the chaos in the home and unable to take in my surroundings for the first few weeks. This lessened considerably during the first visit I had with Victor on his own. Again, I felt discomfort when Anna first breastfed when she seemed to feel anxious about showing me her breast. Her intention was to express some milk in order that Victor would not be left out of the feeding experience from the start.

Women in Search of Women: Clinical Issues That Underlie a Woman's Search for a Female Therapist

Sherly Williams

Sherly Williams

31 Kingsway Road, Evington, Leicester LE5 5TN

Sherly Williams  

Analytic tradition has generally held that the genders of therapist and patient make little difference to transference phenomena. This paper considers a woman's search for a female therapist as an enactment of unconscious hopes, conflicts and anxieties that will gradually become externalised in the here-and-now of the transference relationship. Using clinical material where the starting point of therapy was an expressed need for a female therapist, the paper explores how the gender of the female therapist was used by female patients as raw material for unconscious phantasy concerning their relation to the world, to others and ultimately to themselves.

Commentary by an Analytical Psychologist

Miranda Davies

Miranda Davies

Miranda Davies  

In early 1989 the Association of Child Psychotherapists held a conference called ‘Ways of Seeing’. A video of a baby observation was shown and four speakers were invited to talk about what they saw in the light of their theoretical orientation. The conference was an inquiry into how our theoretical preconceptions inform our observations and, consequently, our clinical practice.

At the conference there seemed to be general agreement about the purpose of baby observation. It is seen as an opportunity to experience through observation the development of a baby in its relationship with its mother and family. Recording the observation, far from attempting to be ‘objective’, is thoroughly informed by empathy and counter-transference. This experience establishes the basis of our understanding of the early development of our patients, and is different from the reconstructed infancy of adults and children in psychotherapy. Equally important, baby observation helps develop skills as an observer, one who offers sympathetic interest while not being active in the situation. The capacity to contain and bear the many intense feelings aroused by the intimate scenes between mother and baby without acting is very important in a budding psychotherapist.

Taking part in a similar though smaller exercise for the British Journal of Psychotherapy, I should like to turn first to the baby observation and then look at the model of the self and its dynamics that has been evolved by Michael Fordham.

Commentary by a Kleinian Child Psychotherapist

Maria Rhode

Maria Rhode

Maria Rhode  

This observation is a convincing and moving example of the transformation that can be brought about in a family by the presence of a sensitive observer, even though this is obviously not the primary task. In this instance, the observer has to bear the pain throughout the visit of being the ‘wrong person’, the sight of whose face represents for the baby the fact of her mother's absence. Being repeatedly the cause of Joanne's crying is particularly distressing for the observer because Victor, the father, is unable to acknowledge that Joanne's unhappiness could have anything to do with his wife's being away at work. He tries everything to soothe Joanne, a bottle, rocking, walking about, a visit to her cot, all without success; guessing at all the possible causes for her crying, from hunger to a full nappy or fatigue. He apologises to the observer for Joanne's behaviour and says to Joanne that her visitor might be ‘disappointed to see her like this when she's usually so good’. The observer replies that ‘I was sorry to see that she was having a tough time today, but that it was a hectic time for everyone and I could see Joanne got fed up sometimes’. Then, after another unsuccessful attempt to explain Joanne's persistent crying by the idea that she might be tired, her father takes her downstairs and walks her around, talking to her for the first time as though she were a human being with feelings as well as ‘a baby’ with physical needs.

While she continued to cry, he walked her around slowly and gently rocking her and soothing her with his quiet voice. He said to her that he guessed that life was not so good for her right now. Slowly, very slowly, she calmed down with her father staring fixedly into her face … She stopped crying and emitted instead deep, soulful sighs.

It does not seem too far-fetched to think that the observer's comment enabled father to change his response to his daughter; but any such comment would probably have sounded hollow if the observer had not throughout the visit endured the pain of being the person who made the baby cry. Indeed, the observer's suggestion earlier on that Joanne might be missing her mother was simply brushed aside: it is possible that father felt it as a reproach though obviously it was not intended as such. (Certainly he was very quick to explain that Joanne was only being given solids to get her used to the taste, as though he were forestalling criticism.) The contrast between the effects of this comment and the observer's enormously enabling remark about Joanne's getting fed up sometimes illustrates beautifully the difference between an accurate explanation that does not address the pain in the situation it describes, and a transforming intervention that grows out of the struggle with this pain. The struggle by this sensitive observer demonstrates one of the reasons infant observation is such excellent preparation for clinical work, apart from any of the knowledge we may derive from it.

The Absent Father in Psychotic Phantasy

David Mann

David Mann

David Mann  

This paper explores the idea that in some psychotic clients their psychosis can be understood as an attempt to form a relationship with an absent father. Some of the literature on the effects of father's absence is discussed and two clients are examined in detail. The conclusion reached is that father's absence is felt by the infant as confirmation of parricidal phantasy. This leads to two processes: (1) the need to make reparation and bring the father back to life and (2) the needs of the psyche to re-establish links with the father in order to achieve psychic homoestasis. Both these processes find expression in psychotic phantasy.

Psychic Contusion: Remarks on Ferenczi and Trauma

Martin Stanton

Martin Stanton

Martin Stanton  

Few would now question that Sandor Ferenczi was an important pioneer in formulating psychoanalytic approaches to trauma. Unfortunately, however, this critical celebration is accompanied by a set of grossly distorted readings of Ferenczi's texts, as well as by serious misrepresentations of his radical transformations of psychoanalytic technique to work with trauma victims. The main distortions are that Ferenczi rediscovered the ‘truth’ of the seduction theory at the end of his life, so advocated that many mental disorders in adult life related to the traumatic experience of sexual abuse in childhood (cf. Masson 1984). Of course, it is neither hard to see why this argument has become so current, given the discovery of the importance and extent of child sexual abuse during the last decade; nor, in this context, is it hard to see why Ferenczi has become characterised as the one analyst who was prepared to say that abuse was real, as opposed to constructed through fantasy, though in fact he said nothing of the sort. Moreover, this view of Ferenczi as the discoverer of the reality of trauma - specifically sexual trauma - has led to equally distorting conceptions of his so-called ‘radical’ revision of psychoanalytic technique to adapt to this increased awareness of real sexual abuse: particularly prevalent here is the notion that he championed empathy, and advocated that analysts should go out of their way to be warm and understanding with their patients in order to facilitate the trust needed for disclosure of the trauma. According to some variants of this view, it is quite acceptable to hug or hold a patient when they are distressed, or to loosen the boundaries between the consulting room and the outside world - such as going for a walk with them or having a conversation in the street, should this be seen as beneficial to building up trust.

In this essay, I wish first of all to discredit this view and show rather that Ferenczi's view of trauma had a much wider focus than child sexual abuse, and in fact centred rather on what is today called Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder. Furthermore, interest in trauma did not suddenly arise or transform with the famous ‘Confusion of Tongues’ paper (1933). Like all the pioneer analysts, Ferenczi's first insights into the nature of trauma came through his acquaintance with the work of Charcot and Bernheim: Ferenczi, like Freud, was particularly concerned with the concept of the idee fixe, the unprocessed amalgam of unconscious material which emerged (usually somatically) in the hypnotic trance or sometimes through therapeutic suggestion to the patient (Stanton 1991). Gazing into Medusa's Eyes: The Fear of Being Seen and Attacks on Insight

Gail Yariv

Gail Yariv

121 York Road, Montpelier, Bristol BS6 5QG

Gail Yariv  

Using a theme from a once weekly therapy I explore the problem of gaining insight when both seeing and being seen are experienced as attack with fears for survival. I use the Oedipus legend to describe narcissistic attacks on sight and the compulsion to return to a rejecting mother. The figures of Hades realm and the story of the Medusa portray the stuck, blind, somatised states I am describing together with the rage, envy and longing involved. I suggest that a cyclic image of movement is useful in the therapy where excessive splitting into opposites with male/female connotations has occurred. Through the theme of eyes, seeing and being blind I develop the relation between critical super-ego penetration and feelings of submission, violation, exposure and shame that induce the need to stay hidden and affect sexual feelings as well as inter and intra-psychic relating.

This is a stimulating and well-researched reference book which offers an original map of the possible relations between feminist critique and psychoanalytic theory. The

496

range of contributors is impressive and includes many outstanding scholars and theorists who offer critical readings and analyses derived from a large number of disciplines. Indeed, one of the most striking elements of this volume is its interdisciplinary character with entries coming from disciplinary spaces as diverse as history, literary studies, criminology, sociology, film studies, women's studies, and philosophy. The overwhelming majority of the contributors work within institutions of higher education, which seems to suggest that universities have become a crucial site for the articulation of relations between ‘feminism and psychoanalysis’ over recent years.

The Dictionary covers both concepts and movements, from bisexuality to sadomasochism via the death drive and from anthropology to postmodernism via écriture féminine, and each entry is followed by a detailed bibliography. Most entries seek to historicise their object of inquiry, offering a very helpful guide to the modifications undergone by different concepts as a result of their contact with a variety of different political and theoretical projects. The organisation of entries is at times a little surprising: separate entries on ‘death drive (Freud)’ and ‘death drive (Lacan)’, each by a different author; while ‘Freud's female patients’ and ‘female analysts’ are contained within the same entry. On the whole, however, the coherence and integrity of each entry is striking.

In any reference work of this nature, the question of the overall integrity of the volume is bound to be both pressing and complex. The rationale behind the Dictionary is explored in Elizabeth Wright's Introduction. Wright offers, in fact, slightly different accounts of the possible relations between ‘feminism’ and ‘psychoanalysis’ and thus suggests a number of different ways of understanding the volume as a whole, and a variety of ways of using it. This may, perhaps, suggest a certain instability in the text as a whole, but this is generally fruitful rather than disabling.
