Sedwell Diggle  

Dr Redfearn has always been a respected and attractive writer because he works from his own extensive clinical and supervisory experience in an especially personal and embodied way. He is also able to think through and articulate some difficult and adventurous psychological ideas in a way which makes them accessible, perhaps for the first time, to his readers who can then make them their own and develop them further in an individual way. The interest and influence of his work have never been confined to the Society of Analytical Psychology, in which for many years he was Director of Training and is still a prominent and active Training Analyst.

In the present volume Dr Redfearn takes on the problem of ‘the almost inherently explosive nature of the human individual’. Since we now have the technological means to bring about the actual destruction of our world, the problem is immediate and urgent. One of the most important general findings in the book emphasises that it is not by striving for, or concentrating on, peace or harmony or moral rightness that a destructive outcome of our human predicament can be averted. That one-sidedness is more likely to contribute to the build-up to real world catastrophe because unrecognised destructive elements, inevitably present in all human beings and groups, will be enacted externally without consciousness or projected outwards onto an enemy against whom it will seem fully justified to go to war with all the means at our disposal. The nuclear threat can be used individually and collectively to avoid taking responsibility for the omnipotent destructive wishes, originating in the hurt and angry feelings of the child, which are part of all of us, recognised or not. These may be displaced onto the image of the bomb itself, which becomes a sort of impersonal scapegoat, or others can be blamed for its existence or deployment.

The relationship between behaviour and consciousness is not a parallel one. It is easier to behave angrily without the hindrance of awareness than knowingly to experience the feeling of anger. Behaviour, Redfearn points out, can be the unconscious. Part of the thesis of the book is that historically we are all engaged in the unconscious enactment of what Redfeam terms ‘myth-realising scenarios’, in increasing danger of bringing about their concrete realisation. Only when we halt the enactment can we experience the meaning of the dream we are living out. Then, painstakingly, we may be able to create ‘a working space between behaviour and mental experience’. In this space we can realise the 'as if quality of the feeling rather than acting directly and unreflectingly. This possibility holds equally for individuals in therapy and for political groups in the world scene.

Clinical Commentary XV

[This section is a regular feature. In this case the two sessions and the therapist's prefacing notes were sent ‘blind’ to three contributors who were asked to comment in a way that would bring out differences between ways of working and of thinking about this particular patient.

Although contributors were asked to give their analytic orientation, according to the house style of the journal, two felt quite independently that such a label would be misleading or an oversimplification - Ed]

The Therapist Writes:

The Patient

Miss X comes to see me once a week. She is in her mid-twenties but looks almost childlike. Her whole appearance conveys a state of deprivation, exacerbated by looking undernourished and thin. Her pale face expresses two things simultaneously: an appeal to be cared for and yet at the same time a withdrawn emptiness which seems to be beyond reach. Terrified of speaking and afraid of taking anything in, she has been a silent patient, sitting in her chair and avoiding eye-contact most of the time. Her silence speaks to me in various ways: sometimes it feels like despair, at other times it has a sullen and angry quality, very often, however, it feels tantalising as if she is involved in some cruel game-playing with me. My countertransference feelings are very strong and can range from acute worries to despair and, in more darker moments, to sheer exasperation.

She was referred by her GP who was worried about her. Miss X went to see him because she felt emotionally dead, at the point of disintegration and frightened that she was losing control of her life. Her GP described her as being in a state of mental and physical retardation and having a very diminished ability to concentrate on anything. Due to her mental state she had been unable to continue her studies and had deferred for twelve months taking her third and final year. A subsequent psychiatrist's assessment confirmed the GP's view of retardation. She was diagnosed as being depressed with no evidence of psychotic processes and psychotherapy was recommended. Its commencement fitted well with her own plans and coincided with resumption of her studies.

John Heaton  

Freedom is a notoriously difficult concept or, rather, maze of concepts, and psychoanalysts have wisely tended to leave it alone. However Kennedy seeks to explore the place of freedom in psychoanalysis, contrasting psychoanalytic notions with philosophical ones.

He claims that the type of freedom which is of most concern in analysis is the freedom to relate since the freedom to act is curtailed. By freedom to relate he means the ability to be close to people without feeling stifled, the ability ‘to be free to want what one wants, and to be free to relate in the way that one wants’. He even speaks of intra-psychic freedom in which one is free to go in and out of the depressive position. He gives several clinical vignettes illustrating how psychoanalysis removes obstacles to freedom, mainly by working through the transference.

A lot of the book is taken up with brief expositions of a number of philosophers and philosophical movements. Thus we have a brief history of hermeneutics in one chapter. In another the author ranges over most of Western philosophy from Plato to Habermas concentrating on notions of reason and freedom.

London

M Davids  

Our cities are increasingly multi-cultural and multi-racial yet this diversity is not reflected in the psychotherapy profession nor in its patient population. In addition, there is a perception that the western-trained therapist is ill equipped to undertake therapy with members of ethnic/cultural minorities (hereafter ‘blacks’). The importance of this book lies in its attempt to place these issues squarely on the agenda. The book is a fitting tribute to the memory of Jafar Kareem - pioneer and campaigner in this field, and founder of Nafsiyat, the intercultural therapy centre - who died unexpectedly a few months after its publication.

The book is made up of twelve thoughtful chapters grouped into three sections - themes, interpretations and practice. It has an appendix of nearly sixty pages of case material for teaching purposes, including suggestions for how it might be used to illuminate the effect of clinicians' stereotypes on clinical thinking. Unfortunately there are no therapy session transcripts. The book ends with an extensive bibliography.

In the first of three ‘themes’ chapters Roland Littlewood presents a historical overview that makes a very good case for taking seriously the provision of psychotherapy services for blacks. Jafar Kareem follows with an account of the orientation of Nafsiyat, giving examples of the sort of patients seen and work done there. His is an approach that takes into account not only the inner world, but also the patient's context and the effect of life in a racist society (the societal transference). Littlewood's second chapter in this section brings a refreshing anthropological perspective to the debate. He shows that although ‘psychological’ distress is recognised and treated universally, its conceptualisation as psychological, and treatment by psycho-therapy, are peculiarly western. Thus, when it comes to the black patient we cannot assume an automatic right to intervene with our psychotherapy. He advocates an intercultural therapy that is especially sensitive to such patients' own constructions of their difficulties. However, this chapter is marred by a distinct anti-psychoanalytic tone to which I shall return.

Val Richards  

‘Tis the same the whole world over;

‘Tis the master who is right.

‘Tis the boy who gets the beating;

Serves the little bugger right!

(p. 150)

For Meltzer, these lines epitomise life in the Claustrum, that rectal compartment which is ‘the heart of this book’. Indeed, it proves quite unnerving to be told that so many of those whom we thought we knew and loved may occupy one or other of the three main Claustrum compartments within the internal mother: the head/breast, the genitals and the rectum. Within each group, with its own dominant trait, brilliant composite portraits emerge, manifested as secretiveness, insincerity and covert contempt respectively. For example, here is a description of people whose ‘entry to the Claustrum was sealed in the latency period’ (p. 86):

Here we find the big, indolent baby boys and the doll's house little girls, for whom the supreme value is comfort. They are voluptuous without eroticism, curious without interest, obedient from inertia and polite without consideration. What they enjoy seems to them what the whole world is striving for, an eternal holiday with companionship but without relationship, in a pretty world without disturbing aesthetic impact. If they have money or an effortless means of earning it, they are content, but their ideal is to be pampered without any recrimination for parasitism….

Meltzer's purpose is to demonstrate how his concept of the Claustrum extends the idea of ‘normal’ projective identification into external objects, to pathological, or intrusive project identification into parts of internal objects. The innovatory aspect of Meltzer's theory is the crucial role of the interior spaces within the internal mother and how this relates to his concept of ‘aesthetic conflict’, which is ‘a tormenting uncertainty about the interior qualities of the aesthetic object’.

Concerned to distinguish between ‘a conception of the inside of the internal mother derived from imagination’ with one that is the product of the omnipotent intrusion, and thereby of omniscience, Meltzer introduces quotations from Paradise Lost and The Odyssey which illustrate how the poetic imagination lends clothing to wholesome, non-intrusive fantasies of the inferior of the internal mother. (In contrast to this, Bosch's triptych, ‘The Garden of Sensual Delights’, which adorns the ‘interior’ of the body of this book, represents the three compartments of the invaded internal mother: indolence (head/breast), sensuality (genitals) and claustrophobia (rectum).)

David Mann  

This is an interesting book that is about more than just Greek tragedy, covering philosophy and politics as well as psychoanalysis. Alford takes the view that the insights of the ancient Greek poets are often more profound than psychoanalysis. Some people may think this is debatable but I for one would not disagree. If the reader is not already familiar with all the extant Greek tragedies a lot of the richness of this book will be missed.

Alford points out that much of the previous psychoanalytic investigation into the Greek poets has merely applied psychoanalytic theories to the plays, seen the theories confirmed and thus pronounced the poets' insights as correct and compatible with or proving psychoanalytic theory. Alford starts with the reverse view: that the plays have something to teach us and that psychoanalysis can be ‘enlarged’ by the tragedies. This means that where important themes in the plays do not seem explicable in psychoanalytic theory, the theory itself is revised to take them into account. The plays set the standard.
